The following description:

**Machine Cause (mcause) register definition**

- The mcause register is an **MXLEN‑bit read‑write register** formatted as shown in Figure 22.  
- **When a trap is taken into M‑mode**, mcause **is written** with a code indicating the event that caused the trap.  
- **Otherwise**, mcause **is never written by the implementation**, though it may be explicitly written by software.  
- The **Interrupt bit** in the mcause register **is set if the trap was caused by an interrupt**.  
- The **Exception Code field** **contains a code identifying the last exception or interrupt**.  
- The Exception Code field **is a WLRL field, so is only guaranteed to hold supported exception codes**.  

**Relation to instruction types**

- **Load and load‑reserved instructions generate load exceptions** (Exception Codes 4–7, 13, 15, etc.).  
- **Store, store‑conditional, and AMO instructions generate store/AMO exceptions** (Exception Codes 6, 7, 15, etc.).  

**Using mcause to separate interrupts from other traps**

- **Interrupts can be separated from other traps with a single branch on the sign of the mcause register value**.  
- **A shift left can remove the interrupt bit and scale the exception codes to index into a trap vector table**.  

**Exception priority and reporting in mcause**

- **If an instruction may raise multiple synchronous exceptions, the decreasing priority order of Table 17 indicates which exception is taken and reported in mcause**.  
- **The priority of any custom synchronous exceptions is implementation‑defined**.  

**mcause values (Table 16)**  

| Interrupt | Exception Code | Description |
|-----------|----------------|-------------|
| 1 | 0 | Reserved |
| 1 | 1 | Supervisor software interrupt |
| 1 | 2 | Reserved |
| 1 | 3 | Machine software interrupt |
| 1 | 4 | Reserved |
| 1 | 5 | Supervisor timer interrupt |
| 1 | 6 | Reserved |
| 1 | 7 | Machine timer interrupt |
| 1 | 8 | Reserved |
| 1 | 9 | Supervisor external interrupt |
| 1 | 10 | Reserved |
| 1 | 11 | Machine external interrupt |
| 1 | 12 | Reserved |
| 1 | 13 | Counter‑overflow interrupt |
| 1 | 14‑15 | Reserved |
| 1 | ≥16 | Designated for platform use |
| 0 | 0 | Instruction address misaligned |
| 0 | 1 | Instruction access fault |
| 0 | 2 | Illegal instruction |
| 0 | 3 | Breakpoint |
| 0 | 4 | Load address misaligned |
| 0 | 5 | Load access fault |
| 0 | 6 | Store/AMO address misaligned |
| 0 | 7 | Store/AMO access fault |
| 0 | 8 | Environment call from U‑mode |
| 0 | 9 | Environment call from S‑mode |
| 0 | 10 | Reserved |
| 0 | 11 | Environment call from M‑mode |
| 0 | 12 | Instruction page fault |
| 0 | 13 | Load page fault |
| 0 | 14 | Reserved |
| 0 | 15 | Store/AMO page fault |
| 0 | 16 | Double trap |
| 0 | 17 | Reserved |
| 0 | 18 | Software check |
| 0 | 19 | Hardware error |
| 0 | 20‑23 | Reserved |
| 0 | 24‑31 | Designated for custom use |
| 0 | 32‑47 | Reserved |
| 0 | 48‑63 | Designated for custom use |
| 0 | ≥64 | Reserved |

**Specific synchronous exceptions that affect mcause**

- **Software‑check exception**: when a software‑check exception is raised, mcause is written with **Interrupt = 0** and **Exception Code = 18**; the x tval register is set either to 0 or to an informative value defined by the raising ISA extension.  
- **Hardware‑error exception**: when a hardware‑error exception is raised, mcause is written with **Interrupt = 0** and **Exception Code = 19**; the x epc register is set to the address of the faulting instruction and the x tval register is set either to 0 or to the virtual address of the fetch/load/store that accessed corrupted data.  

**Interaction with address‑translation and exception priority**

- **When a virtual address is translated into a physical address, the address‑translation algorithm determines which specific exception may be raised**, and the chosen exception (according to Table 17 priority) is the one reported in mcause.  
- **Load/store/AMO address‑misaligned exceptions may have either higher or lower priority than load/store/AMO page‑fault and access‑fault exceptions**; the relative priority is implementation‑defined.  

**Instruction address‑breakpoint handling**

- **Instruction address breakpoints have the same cause value as, but different priority than, data address breakpoints (watchpoints) and environment break exceptions (raised by the EBREAK instruction)**; the breakpoint exception is reported in mcause with **Interrupt = 0** and **Exception Code = 3**.  

**Instruction address‑misaligned exceptions**

- **Instruction address‑misaligned exceptions are raised by control‑flow instructions with misaligned targets**, and are reported in mcause with **Interrupt = 0** and **Exception Code = 0**; these have lower priority than other instruction‑address exceptions.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: mcause is an MXLEN‑bit read‑write register.  
RULE 2: When a trap is taken into M‑mode, mcause is written with a code indicating the event that caused the trap.  
RULE 3: When a trap is not taken into M‑mode, the implementation never writes mcause, although software may write it explicitly.  
RULE 4: The Interrupt bit in mcause is set if the trap was caused by an interrupt.  
RULE 5: The Exception Code field in mcause contains a code identifying the last exception or interrupt.  
RULE 6: The Exception Code field in mcause is a WLRL field and therefore is only guaranteed to hold supported exception codes.  
RULE 7: Load and load‑reserved instructions generate load exceptions whose exception codes (such as 4–7, 13, 15, etc.) are recorded in mcause.  
RULE 8: Store, store‑conditional, and AMO instructions generate store/AMO exceptions whose exception codes (such as 6, 7, 15, etc.) are recorded in mcause.  
RULE 9: Interrupts can be separated from other traps by testing the sign of the mcause value.  
RULE 10: Shifting the mcause value left removes the interrupt bit and scales the exception codes for indexing into a trap vector table.  
RULE 11: If an instruction may raise multiple synchronous exceptions, the decreasing priority order defined in Table 17 determines which exception is taken and reported in mcause.  
RULE 12: The priority of any custom synchronous exceptions reported in mcause is implementation‑defined.  
RULE 13: When a software‑check exception is raised, mcause is written with Interrupt = 0 and Exception Code = 18.  
RULE 14: When a hardware‑error exception is raised, mcause is written with Interrupt = 0 and Exception Code = 19.  
RULE 15: When virtual address translation determines a specific exception, the exception chosen according to Table 17 priority is the one reported in mcause.

The following description:

**Trap‑cause encoding for the mcause register (when the hypervisor extension is implemented)**  

Table 50 lists the possible values of the mcause (and scause) register.  The left‑most column indicates whether the cause is an interrupt (value 1) or an exception (value 0).  The second column gives the numeric cause code, and the third column gives the description used by the architecture.

```
Interrupt | Exception Code | Description
----------+----------------+----------------------------------------------
1         | 0              | Reserved
1         | 1              | Supervisor software interrupt
1         | 2              | Virtual supervisor software interrupt
1         | 3              | Machine software interrupt
1         | 4              | Reserved
1         | 5              | Supervisor timer interrupt
1         | 6              | Virtual supervisor timer interrupt
1         | 7              | Machine timer interrupt
1         | 8              | Reserved
1         | 9              | Supervisor external interrupt
1         | 10             | Virtual supervisor external interrupt
1         | 11             | Machine external interrupt
1         | 12             | Supervisor guest external interrupt
1         | 13             | Counter‑overflow interrupt
1         | 14‑15          | Reserved
1         | ≥16            | Designated for platform use

0         | 0              | Instruction address misaligned
0         | 1              | Instruction access fault
0         | 2              | Illegal instruction
0         | 3              | Breakpoint
0         | 4              | Load address misaligned
0         | 5              | Load access fault
0         | 6              | Store/AMO address misaligned
0         | 7              | Store/AMO access fault
0         | 8              | Environment call from U‑mode or VU‑mode
0         | 9              | Environment call from HS‑mode
0         | 10             | Environment call from VS‑mode
0         | 11             | Environment call from M‑mode
0         | 12             | Instruction page fault
0         | 13             | Load page fault
0         | 14             | Reserved
0         | 15             | Store/AMO page fault
0         | 16             | Double trap
0         | 17             | Reserved
0         | 18             | Software check
0         | 19             | Hardware error
0         | 20             | Instruction guest‑page fault
0         | 21             | Load guest‑page fault
0         | 22             | Virtual instruction
0         | 23             | Store/AMO guest‑page fault
0         | 24‑31          | Designated for custom use
0         | 32‑47          | Reserved
0         | 48‑63          | Designated for custom use
0         | ≥64            | Reserved
```

**Separate ECALL cause values**

* "HS‑mode and VS‑mode ECALLs use different cause values so they can be delegated separately."  
  – Consequently, an environment call from HS‑mode reports cause 9, while an environment call from VS‑mode reports cause 10.

**Virtual‑instruction exception (cause 22)**  

* "When V=1, a virtual‑instruction exception (code 22) is normally raised instead of an illegal‑instruction exception if the attempted instruction is HS‑qualified but is prevented from executing when V=1 either due to insufficient privilege or because the instruction is expressly disabled by a supervisor or hypervisor CSR such as scounteren or hcounteren."  

* "A special rule applies for CSR instructions that access 32‑bit high‑half CSRs such as cycleh and htimedeltah. When V=1 and XLEN=32, an invalid attempt to access a high‑half CSR raises a virtual‑instruction exception instead of an illegal‑instruction exception if the same CSR instruction for the corresponding low‑half CSR (e.g. cycle or htimedelta) is HS‑qualified."  

* "When XLEN>32, an attempt to access a high‑half CSR always raises an illegal‑instruction exception."  

* "Specifically, a virtual‑instruction exception is raised for the following cases:"  

  - **Case 1** – "in VS‑mode, attempts to access a non‑high‑half counter CSR when the corresponding bit in hcounteren is 0 and the same bit in mcounteren is 1;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 2** – "in VS‑mode, if XLEN=32, attempts to access a high‑half counter CSR when the corresponding bit in hcounteren is 0 and the same bit in mcounteren is 1;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 3** – "in VU‑mode, attempts to access a non‑high‑half counter CSR when the corresponding bit in either hcounteren or scounteren is 0 and the same bit in mcounteren is 1;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 4** – "in VU‑mode, if XLEN=32, attempts to access a high‑half counter CSR when the corresponding bit in either hcounteren or scounteren is 0 and the same bit in mcounteren is 1;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 5** – "in VS‑mode or VU‑mode, attempts to execute a hypervisor instruction (HLV, HLVX, HSV, or HFENCE);" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 6** – "in VS‑mode or VU‑mode, attempts to access an implemented non‑high‑half hypervisor CSR or VS CSR when the same access (read/write) would be allowed in HS‑mode, assuming mstatus.TVM=0;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 7** – "in VS‑mode or VU‑mode, if XLEN=32, attempts to access an implemented high‑half hypervisor CSR or high‑half VS CSR when the same access (read/write) to the CSR's low‑half partner would be allowed in HS‑mode, assuming mstatus.TVM=0;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 8** – "in VU‑mode, attempts to execute WFI when mstatus.TW=0, or to execute a supervisor instruction (SRET or SFENCE);" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 9** – "in VU‑mode, attempts to access an implemented non‑high‑half supervisor CSR when the same access (read/write) would be allowed in HS‑mode, assuming mstatus.TVM=0;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 10** – "in VU‑mode, if XLEN=32, attempts to access an implemented high‑half supervisor CSR when the same access to the CSR's low‑half partner would be allowed in HS‑mode, assuming mstatus.TVM=0;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 11** – "in VS‑mode, attempts to execute WFI when hstatus.VTW=1 and mstatus.TW=0, unless the instruction completes within an implementation‑specific, bounded time;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 12** – "in VS‑mode, attempts to execute SRET when hstatus.VTSR=1;" -> mcause is set to 22.  
  - **Case 13** – "in VS‑mode, attempts to execute an SFENCE.VMA or SINVAL.VMA instruction or to access satp, when hstatus.VTVM=1;" -> mcause is set to 22.  

* "Other extensions to the RISC‑V Privileged Architecture may add to the set of circumstances that cause a virtual‑instruction exception when V=1."  

* "On a virtual‑instruction trap, mtval or stval is written the same as for an illegal‑instruction trap."  

**Exception‑priority ordering that determines the value placed in mcause**

* Table 51 defines the synchronous‑exception priority when the hypervisor extension is implemented.  
  – "If an instruction may raise multiple synchronous exceptions, the decreasing priority order of Table 51 indicates which exception is taken and reported in mcause or scause."  

```
Priority   | Exc.Code | Description
-----------+----------+-------------------------------------------------------------
Highest    | 3        | Instruction address breakpoint
           | 12,20,1  | During instruction address translation: first encountered page fault, guest‑page fault, or access fault
           | 1        | With physical address for instruction: instruction access fault
           | 2        | Illegal instruction
           | 22       | Virtual instruction
           | 0        | Instruction address misaligned
           | 8,9,10,11| Environment call
           | 3        | Environment break
           | 3        | Load/store/AMO address breakpoint
           | 4,6      | Optionally: load/store/AMO address misaligned
           | 13,15,21,23,5,7 | During address translation for an explicit memory access: first encountered page fault, guest‑page fault, or access fault
           | 5,7      | With physical address for an explicit memory access: load/store/AMO access fault
Lowest     | 4,6      | If not higher priority: load/store/AMO address misaligned
```

RULE 65: An Instruction address breakpoint (exception code 3) has the highest priority among synchronous exceptions and therefore is reported in mcause when it occurs.  
RULE 66: During instruction address translation, the first encountered page fault (exception code 12), guest‑page fault (exception code 20), or access fault (exception code 1) has priority over lower‑priority exceptions and is reported in mcause.  
RULE 67: An Instruction access fault with a physical address (exception code 1) has priority over illegal‑instruction exceptions and is reported in mcause when it occurs.  
RULE 68: An Illegal instruction exception (exception code 2) has priority over virtual‑instruction exceptions and is reported in mcause when it occurs.  
RULE 69: A Virtual instruction exception (exception code 22) has priority over instruction address misaligned exceptions and is reported in mcause when it occurs.  
RULE 70: An Instruction address misaligned exception (exception code 0) has priority over environment‑call exceptions and is reported in mcause when it occurs.  
RULE 71: Environment call exceptions (exception codes 8, 9, 10, or 11) have priority over environment‑break exceptions and are reported in mcause when they occur.  
RULE 72: An Environment break exception (exception code 3) has priority over load/store/AMO address breakpoint exceptions and is reported in mcause when it occurs.  
RULE 73: A Load/store/AMO address breakpoint exception (exception code 3) has priority over optional load/store/AMO address‑misaligned exceptions and is reported in mcause when it occurs.  
RULE 74: Optional load/store/AMO address‑misaligned exceptions (exception codes 4 or 6) have priority over explicit memory‑access page‑fault or access‑fault exceptions and are reported in mcause when they occur.  
RULE 75: During address translation for an explicit memory access, the first encountered page fault (exception code 13), guest‑page fault (exception code 15), or access fault (exception codes 21 or 23) has priority over load/store/AMO access‑fault exceptions and is reported in mcause when it occurs.  
RULE 76: Load/store/AMO access‑fault exceptions (exception codes 5 or 7) have priority over load/store/AMO address‑misaligned exceptions when no higher‑priority exception is present and are reported in mcause.  
RULE 77: If no higher‑priority exception applies, load/store/AMO address‑misaligned exceptions (exception codes 4 or 6) are reported in mcause.

- The **mcounteren** register is a 32‑bit register that **controls the availability of the hardware performance‑monitoring counters to the next‑lower privileged mode**.

- **When the TM bit in mcounteren is clear**, an attempt to **access the stimecmp or vstimecmp register while executing in a mode less privileged than M** **must cause an illegal‑instruction exception**.

- **When the TM bit in mcounteren is set**, **access to the stimecmp or vstimecmp register is permitted in S‑mode if implemented**, and **access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp) is permitted in VS‑mode if implemented and not otherwise prevented by the TM bit in hcounteren**.

- In harts that implement U‑mode, **mcounteren must be implemented**, but **all fields are WARL and may be read‑only zero**, which **indicates reads to the corresponding counter will cause an illegal‑instruction exception when executing in a less‑privileged mode**.

- In harts **without U‑mode, the mcounteren register should not exist**.

RULE 7: If the TM bit in the mcounteren register is set, access to the vstimecmp register via the stimecmp address is permitted in VS‑mode if VS‑mode is implemented and the TM bit in hcounteren does not otherwise prevent it.

The following description:

- The counter‑inhibit register **mcountinhibit** is a 32‑bit **WARL** register that controls which of the hardware performance‑monitoring counters increment.  

- The settings in **mcountinhibit** only control whether the counters increment; their accessibility is **not** affected by the setting of this register.  

- **When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit in the mcountinhibit register is clear**, the **mcycle**, **minstret**, or **mhpmcounter n** register increments as usual.  

- **When the CY, IR, or HPM n bit in the mcountinhibit register is set**, the corresponding counter does **not** increment.  

- The **mcycle** CSR may be shared between harts on the same core; in that case the **mcountinhibit.CY** field is also shared between those harts, **and writes to mcountinhibit.CY will be visible to those harts**.  

- **If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented**, the implementation behaves **as though the register were set to zero**.  

- Because the **mtime** counter can be shared between multiple cores, it **cannot be inhibited with the mcountinhibit mechanism**.  

- *When the mcycle and minstret counters are not needed, it is desirable to conditionally inhibit them to reduce energy consumption.*  

- *Providing a single CSR to inhibit all counters also allows the counters to be atomically sampled.*
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The mcountinhibit register is a 32‑bit WARL register that controls which hardware performance‑monitoring counters increment.  
RULE 2: Settings in the mcountinhibit register affect only whether the counters increment and do not affect the counters' accessibility.  
RULE 3: When a CY, IR, or HPM n bit in the mcountinhibit register is clear, the corresponding mcycle, minstret, or mhpmcounter n register increments as usual.  
RULE 4: When a CY, IR, or HPM n bit in the mcountinhibit register is set, the corresponding counter does not increment.  
RULE 5: If the mcycle CSR is shared between harts on the same core, the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared between those harts and writes to mcountinhibit.CY are visible to those harts.  
RULE 6: If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as if the register were set to zero.  
RULE 7: The mcountinhibit mechanism does not inhibit the mtime counter, which may be shared between multiple cores.  
RULE 8: It is desirable to conditionally inhibit the mcycle and minstret counters via the mcountinhibit register when they are not needed to reduce energy consumption.  
RULE 9: Providing a single CSR such as mcountinhibit to inhibit all counters also enables the counters to be atomically sampled.

The following description:

- The **machine exception delegation register (medeleg)** is a **64‑bit read/write register**.  
- In harts that implement S‑mode, **medeleg must exist**, and **setting a bit in medeleg will delegate the corresponding trap, when occurring in S‑mode or U‑mode, to the S‑mode trap handler**.  
- In harts that do **not** implement S‑mode, **medeleg should not exist**.  

- **Implementations may subset the delegatable traps**: the set of supported delegatable bits can be discovered by **writing one to every bit location, then reading back the value in medeleg to see which bit positions hold a one**.  

- **Implementations shall not have any bits of medeleg be read‑only one**; i.e., **any synchronous trap that can be delegated must support not being delegated**.  

- **When a trap is delegated to S‑mode via medeleg**, the architectural effect is:  
  - **scause** is written with the trap cause;  
  - **sepc** is written with the virtual address of the instruction that took the trap;  
  - **stval** is written with an exception‑specific datum;  
  - The **SPP** field of **mstatus** is written with the active privilege mode at the time of the trap;  
  - The **SPIE** field of **mstatus** is written with the value of the **SIE** field at the time of the trap;  
  - The **SIE** field of **mstatus** is cleared;  
  - **mcause**, **mepc**, **mtval**, and the **MPP** and **MPIE** fields of **mstatus** are **not written**.  

- **medeleg has a bit position allocated for every synchronous exception shown in Table 16**, with **the index of the bit position equal to the value returned in the mcause register**.  
  - Example: **setting bit 8 allows user‑mode environment calls to be delegated to a lower‑privilege trap handler**.  

- When **XLEN=32**, **medelegh** is a **32‑bit read/write register that aliases bits 63:32 of medeleg**.  
  - **medelegh does not exist when XLEN=64**.  

- For exceptions that **cannot occur in less privileged modes**, the corresponding **medeleg bits should be read‑only zero**.  
  - **medeleg[11] is read‑only zero**.  
  - **medeleg[16] is read‑only zero** (double trap is not delegatable).  

- In versions **1.9.1 and earlier**, these registers **existed but were hardwired to zero in M‑mode only, or M/U without N harts**; there is **no requirement that they return zero in those cases**, as the **misa** register indicates whether they exist.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: medeleg is a 64‑bit read/write register.  
RULE 2: In harts that implement S‑mode, medeleg must exist.  
RULE 3: Setting a bit in medeleg delegates the corresponding trap, when occurring in S‑mode or U‑mode, to the S‑mode trap handler.  
RULE 4: In harts that do not implement S‑mode, medeleg should not exist.  
RULE 5: Implementations shall not have any bits of medeleg be read‑only one; any synchronous trap that can be delegated must support not being delegated.  
RULE 6: When a trap is delegated to S‑mode via medeleg, scause is written with the trap cause.  
RULE 7: When a trap is delegated to S‑mode via medeleg, sepc is written with the virtual address of the instruction that took the trap.  
RULE 8: When a trap is delegated to S‑mode via medeleg, stval is written with an exception‑specific datum.  
RULE 9: When a trap is delegated to S‑mode via medeleg, the SPP field of mstatus is written with the active privilege mode at the time of the trap.  
RULE 10: When a trap is delegated to S‑mode via medeleg, the SPIE field of mstatus is written with the value of the SIE field at the time of the trap.  
RULE 11: When a trap is delegated to S‑mode via medeleg, the SIE field of mstatus is cleared.

The following description:

- **CBO.INVAL – illegal‑instruction exception**  
  If `priv_mode != M` **and** `menvcfg.CBIE == 00` then a *illegal‑instruction exception* is raised.  

- **CBO.INVAL – flush operation**  
  If `priv_mode != M` **and** `menvcfg.CBIE == 01` then the instruction *executes* and performs a **flush** operation.  

- **CBO.INVAL – invalidate operation**  
  If `priv_mode != M` **and** `menvcfg.CBIE` is not `01` (and the illegal‑instruction condition above does not apply) then the instruction *executes* and performs an **invalidate** operation.  

- **CBO.CLEAN / CBO.FLUSH – illegal‑instruction exception**  
  If `priv_mode != M` **and** `menvcfg.CBCFE` is false (`!menvcfg.CBCFE`) then a *illegal‑instruction exception* is raised.  

- **CBO.CLEAN / CBO.FLUSH – normal execution**  
  If `priv_mode != M` **and** `menvcfg.CBCFE` is true then the instruction *executes* (per the "else" clause).  

- **CBO.ZERO – illegal‑instruction exception**  
  If `priv_mode != M` **and** `menvcfg.CBZE` is false (`!menvcfg.CBZE`) then a *illegal‑instruction exception* is raised.  

- **CBO.ZERO – normal execution**  
  If `priv_mode != M` **and** `menvcfg.CBZE` is true then the instruction *executes*.  

- **Independence of xenvcfg fields**  
  The `CBIE`, `CBCFE`, and `CBZE` fields in each `xenvcfg` register *do not affect* the read and write behavior of the same‑named fields in the other `xenvcfg` registers. Consequently, `menvcfg` fields do not affect `senvcfg` or `henvcfg` fields.  

- **WARL property**  
  Each `xenvcfg` register, including `menvcfg`, *is WARL*; software *should determine* the legal values from the execution‑environment discovery mechanism.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: If the current privilege mode is not M and the CBIE field of menvcfg equals 00 then an illegal‑instruction exception is raised.  
RULE 2: If the current privilege mode is not M and the CBIE field of menvcfg equals 01 then the instruction executes and performs a flush operation.  
RULE 3: If the current privilege mode is not M and the CBIE field of menvcfg is not 01 and is not 00 then the instruction executes and performs an invalidate operation.  
RULE 4: If the current privilege mode is not M and the CBCFE field of menvcfg is false then an illegal‑instruction exception is raised.  
RULE 5: If the current privilege mode is not M and the CBCFE field of menvcfg is true then the instruction executes.  
RULE 6: If the current privilege mode is not M and the CBZE field of menvcfg is false then an illegal‑instruction exception is raised.  
RULE 7: If the current privilege mode is not M and the CBZE field of menvcfg is true then the instruction executes.  
RULE 8: The CBIE, CBCFE, and CBZE fields in menvcfg do not affect the read or write behavior of the same‑named fields in senvcfg or henvcfg.  
RULE 9: The menvcfg register is WARL, and software should determine its legal values from the execution‑environment discovery mechanism.

The following description:

- **menvcfg CSR width and access**  
  - The menvcfg CSR is a 64‑bit read/write register.

- **FIOM bit**  
  - If bit **FIOM** is set to one in menvcfg, FENCE instructions executed in modes less privileged than M are modified so the requirement to order accesses to device I/O implies also the requirement to order main memory accesses.  
  - If FIOM=1, for modes less privileged than M, an atomic instruction that accesses a region ordered as device I/O and has its **aq** and/or **rl** bit set is ordered as though it accesses both device I/O and memory.  
  - If S‑mode is not supported, or if **satp.MODE** is read‑only zero (always Bare), the implementation may make FIOM read‑only zero.  

  **Table 18. Modified interpretation of FENCE predecessor and successor sets for modes less privileged than M when FIOM=1**

  | Instruction bit | Meaning when set                                          |
  |-----------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
  | PI              | Predecessor device input and memory reads (PR implied)   |
  | PO              | Predecessor device output and memory writes (PW implied) |
  | SI              | Successor device input and memory reads (SR implied)     |
  | SO              | Successor device output and memory writes (SW implied)   |

- **PBMTE bit**  
  - The **PBMTE** bit controls whether the Svpbmt extension is available for use in S‑mode and G‑stage address translation.  
  - When PBMTE=1, Svpbmt is available for S‑mode and G‑stage address translation.  
  - When PBMTE=0, the implementation behaves as though Svpbmt were not implemented.  
  - If Svpbmt is not implemented, PBMTE is read‑only zero.  
  - For implementations with the hypervisor extension, **henvcfg.PBMTE** is read‑only zero if menvcfg.PBMTE is zero.  
  - After changing menvcfg.PBMTE, executing an **SFENCE.VMA** instruction with **rs1=x0** and **rs2=x0** suffices to synchronize address‑translation caches with respect to the altered interpretation of page‑table entries' PBMT fields.

- **ADUE bit**  
  - If the Svadu extension is implemented, the **ADUE** bit controls whether hardware updating of PTE A/D bits is enabled for S‑mode and G‑stage address translation.  
  - When ADUE=1, hardware updating of PTE A/D bits is enabled during S‑mode address translation, and the implementation behaves as though Svade were not implemented for S‑mode address translation.  
  - When the hypervisor extension is implemented and ADUE=1, hardware updating of PTE A/D bits is enabled during G‑stage address translation, and the implementation behaves as though Svade were not implemented for G‑stage address translation.  
  - When ADUE=0, the implementation behaves as though Svade is implemented for S‑mode and G‑stage address translation.  
  - If Svadu is not implemented, ADUE is read‑only zero.  
  - For implementations with the hypervisor extension, **henvcfg.ADUE** is read‑only zero if menvcfg.ADUE is zero.  
  - After changing menvcfg.ADUE, executing an **SFENCE.VMA** instruction with **rs1=x0** and **rs2=x0** suffices to synchronize address‑translation caches with respect to the altered interpretation of page‑table entries' A/D bits.  
  - The Svade extension requires page‑fault exceptions be raised when PTE A/D bits need be set, hence Svade is implemented when ADUE=0.

- **CDE bit (Counter Delegation Enable)**  
  - When **CDE**=1, the Smcdeleg extension is enabled.  
  - When CDE=0, the Smcdeleg and Ssccfg extensions appear to be not implemented.  
  - If Smcdeleg is not implemented, CDE is read‑only zero.

- **STCE bit (STimecmp Enable)**  
  - When the Sstc extension is not implemented, STCE is read‑only zero.  
  - STCE enables stimecmp for S‑mode when set to one.  
  - When the Sstc extension is implemented and STCE in menvcfg is zero, an attempt to access stimecmp in a mode other than M‑mode raises an illegal‑instruction exception, **henvcfg.STCE** is read‑only zero, and **STIP** in **mip** and **sip** reverts to its defined behavior as if this extension is not implemented.  
  - If the H extension is implemented, then **hip.VSTIP** also reverts its defined behavior as if this extension is not implemented.

- **CBZE field (Cache Block Zero enable)**  
  - When the **CBZE** field is set to 1, it enables execution of the cache block zero instruction **CBO.ZERO** in modes less privileged than M.  
  - Otherwise, the instruction raises an illegal‑instruction exception in modes less privileged than M.  
  - When the Zicboz extension is not implemented, CBZE is read‑only zero.

- **CBCFE field (Cache Block Clean and Flush enable)**  
  - When the **CBCFE** field is set to 1, it enables execution of the cache block clean instruction (**CBO.CLEAN**) and the cache block flush instruction (**CBO.FLUSH**) in modes less privileged than M.  
  - Otherwise, these instructions raise an illegal‑instruction exception in modes less privileged than M.  
  - When the Zicbom extension is not implemented, CBCFE is read‑only zero.

- **CBIE field (Cache Block Invalidate enable, WARL)**  
  - When **CBIE**=00b, the instruction raises an illegal‑instruction exception in modes less privileged than M.  
  - When the Zicbom extension is not implemented, CBIE is read‑only zero.  
  - Encoding 10b is reserved.  
  - When CBIE is set to 01b or 11b, and when enabled for execution in modes less privileged than M, it behaves as follows:  
    - **01b** – The instruction is executed and performs a flush operation, even if configured by a mode less privileged than M to perform an invalidate operation.  
    - **11b** – The instruction is executed and performs an invalidate operation, unless configured by a mode less privileged than M to perform a flush operation.

- **PMM field (Pointer Masking Mode, WARL)**  
  - The **PMM** field enables or disables pointer masking for the next‑lower privilege mode (S‑/HS‑mode if S‑mode is implemented, or U‑mode otherwise), according to Table 19.  
  - If the Smnpm extension is not implemented, PMM is read‑only zero.  
  - The PMM field is read‑only zero for RV32.  

  **Table 19. Legal values of PMM WARL field**

  | Value | Description                                                            |
  |-------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
  | 00    | Pointer masking is disabled (PMLEN = 0)                                |
  | 01    | Reserved                                                               |
  | 10    | Pointer masking is enabled with PMLEN = XLEN‑57 (PMLEN = 7 on RV64)    |
  | 11    | Pointer masking is enabled with PMLEN = XLEN‑48 (PMLEN = 16 on RV64)   |

- **LPE field (Linear Page Extension enable)**  
  - When **LPE**=1 and S‑mode is implemented, the Zicfilp extension is enabled in S‑mode.  
  - If LPE=1 and S‑mode is not implemented, the Zicfilp extension is enabled in U‑mode.  
  - When LPE=0, the Zicfilp extension is not enabled in S‑mode, and the following rules apply to S‑mode:  
    - The hart does not update the ELP state; it remains as **NO_LP_EXPECTED**.  
    - The **LPAD** instruction operates as a no‑op.  
  - If LPE=0 and S‑mode is not implemented, then the same rules apply to U‑mode.

- **SSE field (Speculative Store/Load Enable)**  
  - When **SSE**=1, the Zicfiss extension is activated in S‑mode.  
  - When **SSE**=0, the following rules apply to privilege modes less than M:  
    - 32‑bit Zicfiss instructions revert to their behavior as defined by **Zimop**.  
    - 16‑bit Zicfiss instructions revert to their behavior as defined by **Zcmop**.  
    - The **pte.xwr=010b** encoding in VS/S‑stage page tables becomes reserved.  
    - **SSAMOSWAP.W/D** raises an illegal‑instruction exception.  
  - When menvcfg.SSE is 0, the **henvcfg.SSE** and **senvcfg.SSE** fields are read‑only zero.

- **DTE field (Double‑Trap Enable)**  
  - When **DTE** is zero, the implementation behaves as though the Ssdbltrp extension is not implemented.  
  - When Ssdbltrp is not implemented, **sstatus.SDT**, **vsstatus.SDT**, and **henvcfg.DTE** bits are read‑only zero.

- **menvcfgh register (high half alias)**  
  - When XLEN=32, **menvcfgh** is a 32‑bit read/write register that aliases bits 63:32 of menvcfg.  
  - The menvcfgh register does not exist when XLEN=64.

- **Existence condition**  
  - If U‑mode is not supported, then registers **menvcfg** and **menvcfgh** do not exist.

The following description:

- **menvcfg.SSE field determines xSSE in S‑mode (and HS mode).**  
  *Source:* "When S‑mode is implemented, it is determined as follows: … | S or HS | **menvcfg.SSE** …" (Table 60).

- **xSSE is 0 in M mode, regardless of menvcfg.**  
  *Source:* Table 60 row "M | 0".

- **When S‑mode is not implemented, menvcfg.SSE is not consulted for xSSE; xSSE is 0 at both M and U privilege modes.**  
  *Source:* "When S‑mode is not implemented, then xSSE is 0 at both M and U privilege modes."

- **Changes to the menvcfg.SSE field (which affect xSSE) take effect immediately; address‑translation caches need not be synchronized with SFENCE.VMA, HFENCE.GVMA, or HFENCE.VVMA.**  
  *Source:* "Changes to xSSE take effect immediately; address‑translation caches need not be synchronized with SFENCE.VMA, HFENCE.GVMA, or HFENCE.VVMA instructions."

---

**Table 60 – xSSE determination when S‑mode is implemented**

| Privilege Mode | xSSE        |
|----------------|------------|
| M              | 0          |
| S or HS        | **menvcfg.SSE** |
| VS             | henvcfg.SSE |
| U or VU        | senvcfg.SSE |
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: In S-mode and HS-mode, the architectural xSSE setting is determined by the value of the menvcfg.SSE field.  
RULE 2: In M-mode, the architectural xSSE setting is always 0 regardless of the value of the menvcfg.SSE field.  
RULE 3: If S-mode is not implemented, the menvcfg.SSE field is not consulted for xSSE and the architectural xSSE setting is 0 in both M-mode and U-mode.  
RULE 4: Updates to the menvcfg.SSE field that affect xSSE take effect immediately and do not require address-translation caches to be synchronized with SFENCE.VMA, HFENCE.GVMA, or HFENCE.VVMA instructions.

The following description:

- **Register definition**:  
  *mepc* is an **MXLEN‑bit read/write register** formatted as shown in Figure 21.  

- **Low‑bit constraints**:  
  * The low bit of *mepc* (**mepc[0]**) **is always zero**.  
  * On implementations that support only **IALIGN=32**, the two low bits (**mepc[1:0]**) **are always zero**.  

- **Masking when IALIGN can be 16 or 32**:  
  *If an implementation allows IALIGN to be either 16 or 32 (by changing CSR *misa*, for example), then, whenever **IALIGN=32**, bit **mepc[1]** **is masked on reads so that it appears to be 0**.  
  * This masking **occurs also for the implicit read by the *MRET* instruction**.  
  * Though masked, **mepc[1] remains writable when IALIGN=32**.  

- **WARL property**:  
  * *mepc* **is a WARL register** that **must be able to hold all valid virtual addresses**.  
  * It **need not be capable of holding all possible invalid addresses**.  
  * **Prior to writing *mepc*, implementations may convert an invalid address into some other invalid address that *mepc* is capable of holding**.  

- **Address‑translation independence**:  
  *When address translation is not in effect, virtual addresses and physical addresses are equal. Hence, the **set of addresses *mepc* must be able to represent includes the set of physical addresses that can be used as a valid pc or effective address**.*  

- **Write behavior on traps**:  
  *When a trap is taken into M‑mode, **mepc is written with the virtual address of the instruction that was interrupted or that encountered the exception**.*  
  *Otherwise, **mepc is never written by the implementation**, though it may be explicitly written by software.*
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: mepc is an MXLEN-bit read/write register.  
RULE 2: The least-significant bit of mepc (mepc[0]) is always zero.  
RULE 3: On implementations that support only IALIGN=32, both low bits of mepc (mepc[1] and mepc[0]) are always zero.  
RULE 4: If an implementation permits IALIGN to be either 16 or 32, then when IALIGN=32, bit mepc[1] is masked on reads so that it appears to be zero.  
RULE 5: The read masking of mepc[1] when IALIGN=32 also applies to the implicit read performed by the MRET instruction.  
RULE 6: Although masked on reads when IALIGN=32, bit mepc[1] remains writable.  
RULE 7: mepc is a WARL register that MUST be able to hold all valid virtual addresses.  
RULE 8: mepc need not be capable of holding all possible invalid addresses.  
RULE 9: Prior to writing mepc, implementations MAY convert an invalid address into another invalid address that mepc is capable of holding.  
RULE 10: When address translation is not in effect, the set of addresses that mepc must be able to represent includes all physical addresses that can be used as a valid program counter or effective address.  
RULE 11: When a trap is taken into M-mode, mepc is written with the virtual address of the instruction that was interrupted or that caused the exception.  
RULE 12: In all other circumstances, mepc is never written by the implementation, although software may explicitly write mepc.

The following description:

- **Overflow status bit (OF) in mhpmevent3**  
  *The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software.*  

- **Definition of overflow for mhpmcounter3**  
  *Since hpmcounter values are unsigned values, overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits.*  

- **Behavior after overflow of mhpmcounter3**  
  *Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set.*  

- **Cause of overflow for mhpmcounter3**  
  *Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers.*  

- **Interrupt generation on overflow of mhpmcounter3**  
  *If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.*  
  *If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated.*  
  *Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter.*  

- **Effect of generating a count‑overflow‑interrupt request for mhpmcounter3**  
  *Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit.*  

- **Propagation of OF bit to the local‑interrupt pending register**  
  *When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers.*  

- **Clearing of the pending interrupt bit for mhpmcounter3**  
  *The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows.*  

- **Interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for the count‑overflow interrupt**  
  *The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for this interrupt.*  

- **Delegation of the count‑overflow interrupt**  
  *The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode.*  

- **Enabling overflow interrupt generation for mhpmcounter3**  
  *In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value.*  

- **Re‑initialisation requirement after overflow of mhpmcounter3**  
  *Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.*  

- **Software distinction of newly overflowed counters**  
  *Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow.*  

- **Counting inhibition bits in mhpmevent3**  

  | Bit | Description (as applied to mhpmcounter3) |
  |-----|------------------------------------------|
  | MINH | If set, then counting of events in M‑mode is inhibited |
  | SINH | If set, then counting of events in S/HS‑mode is inhibited |
  | UINH | If set, then counting of events in U‑mode is inhibited |
  | VSINH| If set, then counting of events in VS‑mode is inhibited |
  | VUINH| If set, then counting of events in VU‑mode is inhibited |

  *Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x. All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.*  

  *For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero.*  

- **Shadow copy of OF bit for mhpmcounter3**  
  *If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers.*

The following description:

- **Overflow status (OF) bit** – The OF bit in the *mhpmevent4* register "is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software."  
  *Effect:* When the OF bit for mhpmcounter4 is set, the counter's overflow status is sticky and no further overflow‑interrupt request will be generated until software clears the OF bit.

- **Overflow definition** – "Since hpmcounter values are unsigned values, overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits."  
  *Effect:* An unsigned wrap‑around of the implemented bits of mhpmcounter4 is considered an overflow event.

- **Counter wrap‑around** – "Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set."  
  *Effect:* After mhpmcounter4 overflows, it continues to count (wrapping) while its OF bit stays set.

- **Supervisor‑mode shadow register** – "If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit *scountovf* register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers."  
  *Effect:* The OF status of mhpmcounter4 is reflected in bit 4 of *scountovf* (read‑only) when S‑mode is present.

- **Count‑overflow‑interrupt request generation** – "If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a 'count overflow interrupt request' is generated."  
  *Effect:* If mhpmcounter4 overflows and the OF bit in *mhpmevent4* is zero, a local count‑overflow interrupt is raised.

- **Interrupt suppression** – "If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated."  
  *Effect:* When the OF bit for mhpmcounter4 is set, overflow of mhpmcounter4 does **not** generate a count‑overflow interrupt.

- **Interrupt‑disable function** – "Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter."  
  *Effect:* Setting the OF bit in *mhpmevent4* disables count‑overflow interrupt generation for mhpmcounter4.

- **No overflow from software writes** – "Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers."  
  *Effect:* Writing to *mhpmcounter4* or *mhpmevent4* cannot cause an overflow condition for mhpmcounter4.

- **Local interrupt mapping** – "This count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers."  
  *Effect:* An overflow interrupt generated by mhpmcounter4 sets the LCOFIP (bit 13) pending bit in the appropriate *mip*/*sip* register.

- **Pending‑bit update** – "When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers."  
  *Effect:* After mhpmcounter4 overflows and its OF bit is set, the LCOFIP pending bit will eventually be set.

- **Software clearing of pending bit** – "The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows."  
  *Effect:* Software must clear the LCOFIP pending bit (bit 13) before handling the overflow interrupt for mhpmcounter4.

- **Delegation control** – "The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode."  
  *Effect:* Whether the overflow interrupt from mhpmcounter4 is taken in S‑mode or M‑mode is determined by the *mideleg* register.

- **Interrupt enable/disable via OF bit** – "There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value."  
  *Effect:* To allow mhpmcounter4 to generate another overflow interrupt, software must clear its OF bit and re‑initialize the counter.

- **Re‑initialisation requirement** – "Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated."  
  *Effect:* After mhpmcounter4 overflows, both the counter value and its OF bit must be written to new values before a subsequent overflow interrupt is possible.

- **Software‑maintained active‑mask** – "Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow."  
  *Effect:* An implementation may use a software‑maintained mask that includes mhpmcounter4 to track whether its overflow is pending service.

- **INH bits (mode‑specific counting inhibition)** – The following bits are added to each *mhpmevent* register (including *mhpmevent4*):  

```
| 63 | 62   | 61   | 60   | 59    | 58    | 57   | 56   |
|----|------|------|------|-------|-------|------|------|
| OF | MINH | SINH | UINH | VSINH | VUINH | WPRI | WPRI |
```

  - **MINH** – "If set, then counting of events in M‑mode is inhibited."  
    *Effect:* When MINH in *mhpmevent4* is 1, mhpmcounter4 does not count events while the processor is in M‑mode.

  - **SINH** – "If set, then counting of events in S/HS‑mode is inhibited."  
    *Effect:* When SINH in *mhpmevent4* is 1, mhpmcounter4 does not count events while in S‑mode or HS‑mode.

  - **UINH** – "If set, then counting of events in U‑mode is inhibited."  
    *Effect:* When UINH in *mhpmevent4* is 1, mhpmcounter4 does not count events while in U‑mode.

  - **VSINH** – "If set, then counting of events in VS‑mode is inhibited."  
    *Effect:* When VSINH in *mhpmevent4* is 1, mhpmcounter4 does not count events while in VS‑mode.

  - **VUINH** – "If set, then counting of events in VU‑mode is inhibited."  
    *Effect:* When VUINH in *mhpmevent4* is 1, mhpmcounter4 does not count events while in VU‑mode.

  - **Read‑only zero for unimplemented modes** – "For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero."  

  - **Counting enable condition** – "Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x. All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes."

The following description:

- The **OF bit** in the **mhpmevent5** register *is set when the corresponding hpmcounter (mhpmcounter5) overflows*, and *remains set until written by software*.

- *Overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits* for mhpmcounter5.

- *Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter5 or mhpmevent5 registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers*.

- *If mhpmcounter5 overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.*  
  *If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated.*  
  *Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for mhpmcounter5.*

- *The count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers.*  
  *The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for this interrupt.*

- *Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by mhpmcounter5 sets the associated OF bit.*

- *When an OF bit is set (including the OF bit for mhpmcounter5), it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers.*

- *The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows.*

- *The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode.*

- *If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers, thus includes the OF bit for mhpmcounter5.*

- **INH bits in mhpmevent5** (MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH):  
  - *If set, then counting of events in the corresponding privilege mode (M, S/HS, U, VS, VU) is inhibited for mhpmcounter5.*  
  - *All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes.*  
  - *For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero.*

- **WPRI bits** in mhpmevent5 are *reserved*.

- *There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits.*  
  *Enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value.*  
  *Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.*  
  *These rules apply to mhpmcounter5.*

- *Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow; this includes mhpmcounter5.*
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The OF bit in mhpmevent5 is set when mhpmcounter5 overflows.  
RULE 2: The OF bit in mhpmevent5 remains set until it is written by software.  
RULE 3: Overflow for mhpmcounter5 is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits.  
RULE 4: Count overflow for mhpmcounter5 never results from writes to mhpmcounter5 or mhpmevent5 registers, only from hardware increments.  
RULE 5: If mhpmcounter5 overflows while its OF bit is zero, a count overflow interrupt request is generated.  
RULE 6: If the OF bit for mhpmcounter5 is one, no count overflow interrupt request is generated.  
RULE 7: The OF bit for mhpmcounter5 also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable.  
RULE 8: The count‑overflow‑interrupt request generated by mhpmcounter5 is treated as a standard local interrupt corresponding to bit 13 in the mip, mie, sip, and sie registers.  
RULE 9: The LCOFIP (interrupt‑pending) and LCOFIE (interrupt‑enable) bits in mip/sip and mie/sie respectively correspond to the count‑overflow interrupt generated by mhpmcounter5.  
RULE 10: Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by mhpmcounter5 sets its associated OF bit.  
RULE 11: When the OF bit for mhpmcounter5 is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip and sip registers.  
RULE 12: Software clears the LCOFIP bit before servicing the count overflow interrupt generated by mhpmcounter5.  
RULE 13: The mideleg register determines whether the count‑overflow interrupt generated by mhpmcounter5 is delegated to S‑mode or handled in M‑mode.  
RULE 14: If supervisor mode is implemented, the scountovf register contains a read‑only shadow copy of the OF bit for mhpmcounter5.  
RULE 15: If any INH bit in mhpmevent5 is set, counting of events in the corresponding privilege mode is inhibited for mhpmcounter5.  
RULE 16: If all INH bits in mhpmevent5 are zero, counting of events in all privilege modes is enabled for mhpmcounter5.  
RULE 17: For each INH bit in mhpmevent5, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, that bit is read‑only zero for mhpmcounter5.  
RULE 18: The WPRI bits in mhpmevent5, which are associated with mhpmcounter5, are reserved.  
RULE 19: There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits for mhpmcounter5.  
RULE 20: Enabling overflow interrupt generation for mhpmcounter5 is performed by clearing its OF bit together with initializing the counter to a starting value.  
RULE 21: After mhpmcounter5 has overflowed, both the counter and its OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.  
RULE 22: Software may distinguish newly overflowed mhpmcounter5 (not yet serviced) from already serviced or non‑interrupt‑generating overflowed mhpmcounter5 by maintaining a bit mask of active counters.

The following description:

- The OF bit in **mhpmevent6** "is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software."  
- Since **mhpmcounter6** values are unsigned, "overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits."  
- "There is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set."  

- For each x INH bit in **mhpmevent6**, "if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero."  
- Each x INH bit, "when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x . All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes."  

- "Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers." (applies to **mhpmcounter6**).  

- If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit **scountovf** register "contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers," therefore it also contains a shadow copy of the OF bit for **mhpmevent6**.  

- If **mhpmcounter6** overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, "then a 'count overflow interrupt request' is generated."  
- If the OF bit is one, "then no interrupt request is generated." Consequently, the OF bit "also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter."  

- The count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal "is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers."  
  - The **mip / sip LCOFIP** bits are "the interrupt‑pending bits for this interrupt."  
  - The **mie / sie LCOFIE** bits are "the interrupt‑enable bits for this interrupt." ('LCOFI' represents 'Local Count Overflow Interrupt').  

- "Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit." Therefore, when **mhpmcounter6** generates such a request, its OF bit in **mhpmevent6** is set.  

- When an OF bit is set, "it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers." Thus, after **mhpmcounter6** overflows and sets its OF bit, the corresponding LCOFIP bit will eventually be set.  

- The **LCOFIP** bit "is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows."  

- The **mideleg** register "controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode."  

- "Enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value." Therefore, to enable overflow interrupt generation for **mhpmcounter6**, software must clear the OF bit in **mhpmevent6** and initialize **mhpmcounter6**.  

- "Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated." Hence, after **mhpmcounter6** overflows, both **mhpmcounter6** and its OF bit must be reinitialized to allow a subsequent overflow interrupt.  

- Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced) from already serviced or non‑interrupting overflowed counters "by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow." This applies to **mhpmcounter6** as one of the counters tracked by such a mask.

RULE 3: After mhpmcounter6 overflows, the counter wraps around and continues counting while the sticky OF bit in mhpmevent6 remains set, resulting in no loss of information.  
RULE 4: For each privilege mode x, if the privilege mode is not implemented, the corresponding x INH bit in mhpmevent6 for mhpmcounter6 is read‑only zero.  
RULE 5: When an x INH bit in mhpmevent6 for mhpmcounter6 is set, counting of events for mhpmcounter6 is inhibited while executing in privilege mode x, and when all x INH bits are zero, mhpmcounter6 counts events in all privilege modes.

RULE 8: If mhpmcounter6 overflows while its associated OF bit in mhpmevent6 is zero, a count overflow interrupt request is generated.

- The hardware‑performance monitor provides 29 additional 64‑bit event counters, **mhpmcounter3 – mhpmcounter31**; therefore **mhpmcounter7** is one of these counters and is a 64‑bit counter.

- A legal implementation may choose to make **mhpmcounter7** and its corresponding selector **mhpmevent7** *read‑only zero*. In such an implementation, reads of **mhpmcounter7** return 0 and writes have no effect.  

- When **XLEN = 32**:

  * A write to **mhpmcounter7** changes **only bits 31‑0** of the counter.  
  * A read of **mhpmcounter7h** (the high‑half CSR) returns **bits 63‑32** of the counter.  
  * A write to **mhpmcounter7h** changes **only bits 63‑32** of the counter.  

- The above behavior for the low‑half (**mhpmcounter7**) and high‑half (**mhpmcounter7h**) CSRs applies only when the **Sscofpmf** extension is implemented for the high‑half CSRs (the text specifies this requirement for the **mhpmevent** high‑half CSRs; the same requirement is implied for the counter high‑half CSRs).

The following description:

- The **OF bit** in *mhpmevent7* "is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software."  
  *Effect:* When *mhpmcounter7* overflows, its associated OF bit becomes 1 and stays 1 until software clears it.

- **Overflow definition:** "Since hpmcounter values are unsigned values, overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits."  
  *Effect:* An overflow of *mhpmcounter7* occurs when its unsigned value wraps past the most‑significant implemented bit.

- **Counter wrap‑around:** "Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set."  
  *Effect:* After *mhpmcounter7* overflows, it continues counting from zero (or the wrapped value) while its OF bit stays set.

- **Supervisor shadow register:** "If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers."  
  *Effect:* The OF bit for *mhpmevent7* is reflected as a read‑only bit in *scountovf*.

- **Count‑overflow interrupt generation:**  
  – "If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a 'count overflow interrupt request' is generated."  
  – "If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated."  
  *Effect:* When *mhpmcounter7* overflows and its OF bit is 0, a count‑overflow interrupt request is raised; if the OF bit is already 1, no interrupt request is raised.

- **Interrupt‑disable role of OF:** "Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter."  
  *Effect:* Setting the OF bit in *mhpmevent7* disables further overflow interrupt requests for *mhpmcounter7*.

- **Source of overflow:** "Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers."  
  *Effect:* *mhpmcounter7* can overflow only due to hardware increments, never due to a software write to *mhpmcounter7* or *mhpmevent7*.

- **Local interrupt mapping:** "This count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers. The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for this interrupt."  
  *Effect:* An overflow interrupt generated by *mhpmcounter7* sets LCOFIP (bit 13) in *mip*/*sip* and is enabled/disabled by LCOFIE in *mie*/*sie*.

- **Setting of OF and pending bit:** "Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit. When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers."  
  *Effect:* When *mhpmcounter7* causes an overflow interrupt, its OF bit is set and later the LCOFIP bit becomes pending.

- **Clearing of pending bit:** "The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows."  
  *Effect:* Software must clear the LCOFIP bit (bit 13) before handling the overflow interrupt caused by *mhpmcounter7*.

- **Interrupt delegation:** "The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode."  
  *Effect:* Whether the overflow interrupt from *mhpmcounter7* is handled in S‑mode or M‑mode is determined by *mideleg*.

- **No separate enable bit:** "There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits. In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value."  
  *Effect:* To allow *mhpmcounter7* to generate another overflow interrupt, software must clear its OF bit and re‑initialize the counter.

- **Re‑initialization requirement:** "Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated."  
  *Effect:* After *mhpmcounter7* overflows, both the counter value and its OF bit must be written to restart overflow‑interrupt generation.

- **Software masking of active counters:** "Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow."  
  *Effect:* Software may track *mhpmcounter7* in a bit mask to know whether it is awaiting service or has been handled.

- **INH bits in mhpmevent7:**  
  – "MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH … inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x. All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes."  
  – "For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero."  
  *Effect:* Setting any INH bit in *mhpmevent7* (e.g., MINH) stops *mhpmcounter7* from counting events when the processor is in the corresponding privilege mode; if the mode is unimplemented, the bit reads as zero.

The following description:

- **mhpmcounter8 overflow status bit (OF) definition** – In the mhpmevent register that controls mhpmcounter8, bit 63 is named **OF** and is described as "Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows"【source】.

- **When the OF bit is set** – "When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers"【source】.

- **When the OF bit is cleared** – "If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a 'count overflow interrupt request' is generated"【source】.

- **When the OF bit is one** – "If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated"【source】.

- **OF bit as interrupt‑disable** – "Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter"【source】.

- **OF bit set on overflow** – "The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software"【source】.

- **Unsigned overflow definition** – "Since hpmcounter values are unsigned values, overflow is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits"【source】.

- **Counter wrap‑around after overflow** – "Note that there is no loss of information after an overflow since the counter wraps around and keeps counting while the sticky OF bit remains set"【source】.

- **Count‑overflow‑interrupt request generation** – "Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit"【source】.

- **Interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits** – "The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for this interrupt"【source】.

- **Local interrupt mapping** – "The count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers"【source】.

- **Interrupt delegation** – "The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode"【source】.

- **No separate overflow status and enable bits** – "There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits"【source】.

- **Enabling overflow interrupt generation** – "In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value"【source】.

- **Reinitialisation requirement after overflow** – "Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated"【source】.

- **Overflow never caused by software writes** – "Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers"【source】.

- **Supervisor‑mode shadow copy of OF bits** – "If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers" (applies to the OF bit that controls mhpmcounter8)【source】.

- **INH bits inhibit counting in specific privilege modes** – "Each of the five x INH bits, when set, inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x. All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes" (the INH bits are in the mhpmevent register that controls mhpmcounter8)【source】.

- **Unimplemented privilege mode INH bits read‑only zero** – "For each x INH bit, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero" (affects counting behavior of mhpmcounter8)【source】.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: Bit 63 of the mhpmcounter8 mhpmevent register is named OF and functions as an overflow status and interrupt‑disable bit that is set when the mhpmcounter8 overflows.  
RULE 2: When the OF bit in the mhpmcounter8 mhpmevent register is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip and sip registers.  
RULE 3: If mhpmcounter8 overflows while its OF bit is zero, a count‑overflow‑interrupt request is generated.  
RULE 4: If the OF bit in the mhpmcounter8 mhpmevent register is one, no count‑overflow‑interrupt request is generated.  
RULE 5: The OF bit in the mhpmcounter8 mhpmevent register functions as a count‑overflow‑interrupt disable for mhpmcounter8.  
RULE 6: The OF bit in the mhpmcounter8 mhpmevent register is set when mhpmcounter8 overflows and remains set until written by software.  
RULE 7: Overflow of mhpmcounter8 is defined as unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits of mhpmcounter8.  
RULE 8: After mhpmcounter8 overflows, the counter wraps around and continues counting while the sticky OF bit remains set, resulting in no loss of information.  
RULE 9: Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by mhpmcounter8 sets its OF bit.  
RULE 10: The LCOFIP bits in the mip and sip registers are the interrupt‑pending bits and the LCOFIE bits in the mie and sie registers are the interrupt‑enable bits for the mhpmcounter8 overflow interrupt.  
RULE 11: The mhpmcounter8 overflow interrupt request is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip, mie, sip, and sie registers.  
RULE 12: The mideleg register controls delegation of the mhpmcounter8 overflow interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode.

RULE 15: After mhpmcounter8 has overflowed, both mhpmcounter8 and its OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.  
RULE 16: Count overflow of mhpmcounter8 never results from writes to the mhpmcounter8 or its mhpmevent8 register, only from hardware increments of mhpmcounter8.  
RULE 17: If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains a read‑only shadow copy of the OF bit for mhpmcounter8.  
RULE 18: Each of the five x INH bits in the mhpmcounter8 mhpmevent register, when set, inhibits counting of events while the processor is in privilege mode x.  
RULE 19: If all five x INH bits in the mhpmcounter8 mhpmevent register are zero, counting of events occurs in all privilege modes.  
RULE 20: If a privilege mode x is not implemented, the corresponding x INH bit in the mhpmcounter8 mhpmevent register is read‑only zero.

- **mhpmcounter9 is a hardware performance‑monitoring counter.**

- **Read‑only shadow CSR:**  
  "The cycle, instret, and **hpmcountern** CSRs are read‑only shadows of **mcycle**, **minstret**, and **mhpmcounter n**, respectively."  
  Consequently, the CSR **hpmcountern** with *n = 9* (i.e., **hpmcounter9**) provides a read‑only view of **mhpmcounter9**.

- **High‑word shadow for XLEN=32:**  
  "When XLEN=32, the … **hpmcounternh** CSRs are read‑only shadows of **mhpmcounternh**, respectively."  
  Therefore, for XLEN=32 the CSR **hpmcounter9h** is the read‑only shadow of the upper 32 bits of **mhpmcounter9**.

- **Accessibility controlled by mcounteren.HPM9 bit:**  
  "When the CY, TM, IR, or **HPM n** bit in the **mcounteren** register is clear, attempts to read the … **hpmcountern** register while executing in S‑mode or U‑mode will cause an illegal‑instruction exception. When one of these bits is set, access to the corresponding register is permitted in the next implemented privilege mode (S‑mode if implemented, otherwise U‑mode)."  
  Applying this to *n = 9*:  
  * If the **HPM9** bit in **mcounteren** is **clear**, an attempt to read **hpmcounter9** (the shadow of **mhpmcounter9**) while executing in S‑mode or U‑mode **must cause an illegal‑instruction exception**.  
  * If the **HPM9** bit is **set**, access to **hpmcounter9** **is permitted** in the next lower implemented privilege mode.

- **Counters continue to increment regardless of accessibility:**  
  "The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible."  
  Hence, **mhpmcounter9** **continues to increment** even when its shadow CSR is inaccessible due to the **HPM9** bit being clear.
