The following description:

**Bits added to each mhpmevent register (including mhpmevent28)**  

| Bit | Field | Description (as defined for mhpmevent28) |
|-----|-------|------------------------------------------|
| 63  | OF    | Overflow status and interrupt‑disable bit that is set when counter overflows |
| 62  | MINH  | If set, then counting of events in M‑mode is inhibited |
| 61  | SINH  | If set, then counting of events in S/HS‑mode is inhibited |
| 60  | UINH  | If set, then counting of events in U‑mode is inhibited |
| 59  | VSINH | If set, then counting of events in VS‑mode is inhibited |
| 58  | VUINH | If set, then counting of events in VU‑mode is inhibited |
| 57  | WPRI  | Reserved |
| 56  | WPRI  | Reserved |

**Behavior of the INH bits in mhpmevent28**  

- For each x INH bit (MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH), *if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero*.  
- When an INH bit is set, it *inhibits counting of events while in the corresponding privilege mode*.  
- If all five INH bits are zero, *counting of events occurs in all modes*.

**Behavior of the OF bit in mhpmevent28**  

- The OF bit *is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows* and *remains set until written by software*.  
- Overflow is defined as *unsigned overflow of the implemented counter bits* of the associated hpmcounter.  
- After an overflow, *the counter wraps around and continues counting while the sticky OF bit remains set* (no loss of information).  

**Interaction with other registers**  

- If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit **scountovf** register *contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers*, therefore it also shadows the OF bit of mhpmevent28.  

**Count‑overflow‑interrupt generation related to mhpmevent28**  

- *If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated.*  
- *If the OF bit is one, no interrupt request is generated.*  
- Consequently, *the OF bit also functions as a count‑overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter*.  

- *Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers* (thus writes to mhpmevent28 do not cause overflow).  

- The count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal *is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip/mie/sip/sie registers*.  
  - The mip/sip **LCOFIP** and mie/sie **LCOFIE** bits are, respectively, the *interrupt‑pending* and *interrupt‑enable* bits for this interrupt (LCOFI = "Local Count Overflow Interrupt").  

- *Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit*.  
- *When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip/sip registers*.  
- *The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows*.  
- *The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode*.  

- *There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits*.  
- *Enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value*.  
- *Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated*.  

**Software distinction of overflow status for mhpmevent28**  

- *Software can distinguish newly overflowed counters (yet to be serviced by an overflow interrupt handler) from overflowed counters that have already been serviced or that are configured to not generate an interrupt on overflow, by maintaining a bit mask reflecting which counters are active and due to eventually overflow*.  

These statements constitute all explicit, normative and descriptive information in the source text that directly concerns the behavior of the **mhpmevent28** register.

The following description:

- The mhpmevent29 register contains the eight bits **OF**, **MINH**, **SINH**, **UINH**, **VSINH**, **VUINH**, **WPRI**, **WPRI** as shown in the table in §21.1.  
- **OF**: "Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows." The OF bit **is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows**, and **remains set until written by software**.  
- **MINH**, **SINH**, **UINH**, **VSINH**, **VUINH**: each is an "INH" bit. For each **x INH** bit, "if set, then counting of events … is inhibited" in the associated privilege mode (M, S/HS, U, VS, VU respectively). "All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes."  
- For each **x INH** bit, "if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero."  
- The two **WPRI** bits are reserved.  

**Direct consequences of the OF bit in mhpmevent29**

- If an hpmcounter29 overflows **while the associated OF bit is zero**, then a *count overflow interrupt request* is generated.  
- If the OF bit is one, **no interrupt request is generated**. Therefore the OF bit also functions as a count‑overflow interrupt disable for hpmcounter29.  
- When a count‑overflow‑interrupt request is generated, the **OF bit is set** and "eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers."  
- The LCOFIP bit is the "local count overflow interrupt‑pending" bit (bit 13) and is cleared by software before servicing the overflow interrupt.  

**Interaction with other registers**

- If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit **scountovf** register "contains read‑only shadow copies of the OF bits in all 29 mhpmevent registers," therefore it contains a shadow copy of **mhpmevent29.OF**.  
- The **mideleg** register "controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode"; this delegation applies to the interrupt generated by overflow of hpmcounter29.  

**Additional architectural rules affecting mhpmevent29**

- "Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers." Hence writing to **mhpmevent29** does **not** cause an overflow.  
- "Enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value." Consequently, to enable a new overflow interrupt for hpmcounter29, software must clear **mhpmevent29.OF** and re‑initialize the counter.  
- "Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated." This applies to hpmcounter29 and **mhpmevent29.OF**.  

**Summary of behavior specific to mhpmevent29**

| Bit | Effect (as stated) |
|-----|--------------------|
| OF  | Set on overflow of the associated hpmcounter29; remains set until written; disables overflow interrupt when set; generates LCOFIP when overflow occurs with OF=0. |
| MINH| When set, inhibits counting of events in M‑mode for counter29. |
| SINH| When set, inhibits counting of events in S/HS‑mode for counter29. |
| UINH| When set, inhibits counting of events in U‑mode for counter29. |
| VSINH| When set, inhibits counting of events in VS‑mode for counter29. |
| VUINH| When set, inhibits counting of events in VU‑mode for counter29. |
| WPRI| Reserved (no defined effect). |

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The mhpmevent29 register is an eight‑bit register containing the fields OF, MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH, and two WPRI bits.  
RULE 2: The OF bit in mhpmevent29 is set when the associated hpmcounter29 overflows and remains set until written by software.  
RULE 3: If hpmcounter29 overflows while the OF bit in mhpmevent29 is zero, a count‑overflow interrupt request is generated.  
RULE 4: If the OF bit in mhpmevent29 is one, no count‑overflow interrupt request is generated for an overflow of hpmcounter29.  
RULE 5: When a count‑overflow interrupt request is generated for hpmcounter29, the OF bit in mhpmevent29 is set.  
RULE 6: After the OF bit in mhpmevent29 is set by a count‑overflow interrupt request, the LCOFIP bit in the mip or sip registers is eventually set but not necessarily immediately.  
RULE 7: The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the overflow interrupt generated by mhpmevent29.  
RULE 8: If supervisor mode is implemented, the 32‑bit scountovf register contains a read‑only shadow copy of the OF bit in mhpmevent29.  
RULE 9: The mideleg register controls delegation of the overflow interrupt generated by hpmcounter29, which is the interrupt associated with the OF bit in mhpmevent29.  
RULE 10: Writes to mhpmevent29 do not cause a count overflow; count overflow only results from hardware increments of the counter registers.  
RULE 11: Enabling overflow interrupt generation for hpmcounter29 is performed by clearing the OF bit in mhpmevent29 in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value.  
RULE 12: After hpmcounter29 has overflowed, both the counter and the OF bit in mhpmevent29 MUST be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated.  
RULE 13: The MINH bit in mhpmevent29, when set, inhibits counting of events for hpmcounter29 in machine mode.  
RULE 14: The SINH bit in mhpmevent29, when set, inhibits counting of events for hpmcounter29 in supervisor/hypervisor mode.  
RULE 15: The UINH bit in mhpmevent29, when set, inhibits counting of events for hpmcounter29 in user mode.  
RULE 16: The VSINH bit in mhpmevent29, when set, inhibits counting of events for hpmcounter29 in virtual‑supervisor mode.  
RULE 17: The VUINH bit in mhpmevent29, when set, inhibits counting of events for hpmcounter29 in virtual‑user mode.  
RULE 18: If all INH bits (MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH) in mhpmevent29 are zero, counting of events for hpmcounter29 occurs in all privilege modes.  
RULE 19: For each INH bit in mhpmevent29, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, that bit is read‑only zero.  
RULE 20: The two WPRI bits in mhpmevent29 are reserved and have no defined effect.

The following description:

- The bits **OF, MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH, WPRI, WPRI** are added to **mhpmevent30**.  
  - **OF** – "Overflow status and interrupt disable bit that is set when counter overflows".  
  - **MINH** – "If set, then counting of events in M‑mode is inhibited".  
  - **SINH** – "If set, then counting of events in S/HS‑mode is inhibited".  
  - **UINH** – "If set, then counting of events in U‑mode is inhibited".  
  - **VSINH** – "If set, then counting of events in VS‑mode is inhibited".  
  - **VUINH** – "If set, then counting of events in VU‑mode is inhibited".  
  - **WPRI** – "Reserved".

- **For each x INH bit**, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, **the bit is read‑only zero** (applies to the MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH bits of mhpmevent30).

- **Each of the five x INH bits**, when set, **inhibit counting of events while in privilege mode x**. **All‑zeroes for these bits results in counting of events in all modes** (applies to mhpmevent30).

- **The OF bit is set when the corresponding hpmcounter overflows, and remains set until written by software** (applies to the OF bit of mhpmevent30).

- **If an hpmcounter overflows while the associated OF bit is zero, then a "count overflow interrupt request" is generated** (applies to the hpmcounter30 associated with mhpmevent30).

- **If the OF bit is one, then no interrupt request is generated** (applies to mhpmevent30).

- **Consequently the OF bit also functions as a count overflow interrupt disable for the associated hpmcounter** (applies to mhpmevent30).

- **Count overflow never results from writes to the mhpmcounter n or mhpmevent n registers, only from hardware increments of counter registers** (applies to mhpmevent30).

- **This count‑overflow‑interrupt‑request signal is treated as a standard local interrupt that corresponds to bit 13 in the mip / mie / sip / sie registers** (the interrupt generated by overflow of hpmcounter30 associated with mhpmevent30 follows this rule).

- **The mip / sip LCOFIP and mie / sie LCOFIE bits are, respectively, the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for this interrupt** (the interrupt caused by mhpmevent30's OF bit uses these bits).

- **Generation of a count‑overflow‑interrupt request by an hpmcounter sets the associated OF bit** (when hpmcounter30 overflows, the OF bit in mhpmevent30 is set).

- **When an OF bit is set, it eventually, but not necessarily immediately, sets the LCOFIP bit in the mip / sip registers** (applies to the OF bit of mhpmevent30).

- **The LCOFIP bit is cleared by software before servicing the count overflow interrupt resulting from one or more count overflows** (relevant to the interrupt generated by mhpmevent30).

- **The mideleg register controls the delegation of this interrupt to S‑mode versus M‑mode** (the overflow interrupt associated with mhpmevent30 is delegated according to mideleg).

- **There are not separate overflow status and overflow interrupt enable bits** (the OF bit in mhpmevent30 serves both purposes).

- **In practice, enabling overflow interrupt generation (by clearing the OF bit) is done in conjunction with initializing the counter to a starting value** (software must clear the OF bit of mhpmevent30 when initializing the associated counter).

- **Once a counter has overflowed, it and the OF bit must be reinitialized before another overflow interrupt can be generated** (applies to hpmcounter30 and the OF bit of mhpmevent30).

The following description:

- The machine interrupt delegation (mideleg) register is an MXLEN‑bit read/write register.  

- In harts with S‑mode, the medeleg and mideleg registers **must** exist, and **setting a bit in medeleg or mideleg will delegate the corresponding trap, when occurring in S‑mode or U‑mode, to the S‑mode trap handler**.  

- In harts without S‑mode, the medeleg and mideleg registers **should** not exist.  

- An implementation can choose to subset the delegatable traps, **with the supported delegatable bits found by writing one to every bit location, then reading back the value in medeleg or mideleg to see which bit positions hold a one**.  

- An implementation **shall not** fix as read‑only one any bits of mideleg **corresponding to machine‑level interrupts** (but may do so for lower‑level interrupts).  

- Version 1.11 and earlier **prohibited having any bits of mideleg be read‑only one**. Platform standards may always add such restrictions.  

- **Delegated interrupts result in the interrupt being masked at the delegator privilege level**. For example, **if the supervisor timer interrupt (STI) is delegated to S‑mode by setting mideleg[5], STIs will not be taken when executing in M‑mode**. **By contrast, if mideleg[5] is clear, STIs can be taken in any mode and regardless of current mode will transfer control to M‑mode**.  

- mideleg **holds trap delegation bits for individual interrupts, with the layout of bits matching those in the mip register** (i.e., **STIP interrupt delegation control is located in bit 5**).
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The mideleg register is an MXLEN‑bit read/write register.  
RULE 2: In harts that implement S‑mode, the mideleg register must exist.  
RULE 3: In harts that implement S‑mode, setting a bit in mideleg delegates the corresponding trap that occurs in S‑mode or U‑mode to the S‑mode trap handler.  
RULE 4: In harts that do not implement S‑mode, the mideleg register should not exist.  
RULE 5: An implementation may support only a subset of delegatable traps, and the supported delegatable bits in mideleg can be discovered by writing one to every bit position of mideleg and then reading back the value to see which bit positions retain a one.  
RULE 6: An implementation shall not make any bits of mideleg that correspond to machine‑level interrupts read‑only one.  
RULE 7: An implementation may make bits of mideleg that correspond to lower‑level interrupts read‑only one.  
RULE 8: Versions of the specification up to and including 1.11 prohibited any bits of mideleg from being read‑only one.  
RULE 9: Delegated interrupts are masked at the delegator privilege level as indicated by mideleg.  
RULE 10: If the supervisor timer interrupt is delegated to S‑mode by setting mideleg[5], the supervisor timer interrupt will not be taken while executing in M‑mode.  
RULE 11: If mideleg[5] is clear, the supervisor timer interrupt can be taken in any mode and will always transfer control to M‑mode regardless of the current mode.  
RULE 12: The bits in mideleg correspond to individual interrupt delegation controls and have the same layout as the bits in the mip register.  
RULE 13: The delegation control for the supervisor timer interrupt is located in bit 5 of mideleg.

The following description:

- **M‑mode uses the mideleg CSR to delegate some traps to HS‑mode.**  
  *Source:* "M‑mode usually uses the medeleg and mideleg CSRs to delegate some traps to HS‑mode."  

- **An interrupt that has been delegated to HS‑mode (using mideleg) is further delegated to VS‑mode if the corresponding hideleg bit is set.**  
  *Source:* "An interrupt that has been delegated to HS‑mode (using mideleg) is further delegated to VS‑mode if the corresponding hideleg bit is set."  

- **Bits of hideleg that control further delegation of interrupts originally delegated by mideleg:**  
  - Bits 10, 6, 2 (the standard VS‑level interrupts) are **writable**.  
  - Bits 12, 9, 5, 1 (the standard S‑level interrupts) are **read‑only zeros**.  
  *Source:* "Among bits 15:0 of hideleg, bits 10, 6, and 2 (corresponding to the standard VS‑level interrupts) are writable, and bits 12, 9, 5, and 1 (corresponding to the standard S‑level interrupts) are read‑only zeros."  

- **Translation that occurs when an interrupt delegated via mideleg (and then hideleg) reaches VS‑mode:**  
  - When a **virtual supervisor external interrupt (code 10)** is delegated to VS‑mode, the machine automatically translates it into a **supervisor external interrupt (code 9)** for VS‑mode, including the value written to vscause on an interrupt trap.  
  - When a **virtual supervisor timer interrupt (code 6)** is delegated to VS‑mode, it is translated into a **supervisor timer interrupt (code 5)** for VS‑mode.  
  - When a **virtual supervisor software interrupt (code 2)** is delegated to VS‑mode, it is translated into a **supervisor software interrupt (code 1)** for VS‑mode.  
  - Similar translations **may or may not be done** for platform interrupt causes (codes 16 and above).  
  *Source:* "When a virtual supervisor external interrupt (code 10) is delegated to VS‑mode, it is automatically translated by the machine into a supervisor external interrupt (code 9) for VS‑mode, including the value written to vscause on an interrupt trap. Likewise, a virtual supervisor timer interrupt (6) is translated into a supervisor timer interrupt (5) for VS‑mode, and a virtual supervisor software interrupt (2) is translated into a supervisor software interrupt (1) for VS‑mode. Similar translations may or may not be done for platform interrupt causes (codes 16 and above)."
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: M‑mode usually uses the mideleg CSR to delegate some traps to HS‑mode.  
RULE 2: An interrupt that has been delegated to HS‑mode using mideleg is further delegated to VS‑mode if the corresponding hideleg bit is set.  
RULE 3: When an interrupt is delegated to HS‑mode via mideleg, the corresponding hideleg bits 10, 6, and 2 (the standard VS‑level interrupts) are writable.  
RULE 4: When an interrupt is delegated to HS‑mode via mideleg, the corresponding hideleg bits 12, 9, 5, and 1 (the standard S‑level interrupts) are read‑only zeros.  
RULE 5: When a virtual supervisor external interrupt (code 10) is delegated to HS‑mode using mideleg and then delegated to VS‑mode, the machine automatically translates it into a supervisor external interrupt (code 9) for VS‑mode and includes the value written to vscause on the interrupt trap.  
RULE 6: When a virtual supervisor timer interrupt (code 6) is delegated to HS‑mode using mideleg and then delegated to VS‑mode, the machine translates it into a supervisor timer interrupt (code 5) for VS‑mode.  
RULE 7: When a virtual supervisor software interrupt (code 2) is delegated to HS‑mode using mideleg and then delegated to VS‑mode, the machine translates it into a supervisor software interrupt (code 1) for VS‑mode.  
RULE 8: Similar translations may or may not be performed for platform interrupt causes (codes 16 and above) that are delegated via mideleg and then hideleg.

- mie is the corresponding MXLEN‑bit read/write register containing interrupt enable bits.

- Bits mip.MEIP and **mie.MEIE** are the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for machine‑level external interrupts.  

- Bits mip.MTIP and **mie.MTIE** are the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for machine timer interrupts.  

- Bits mip.MSIP and **mie.MSIE** are the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for machine‑level software interrupts.

- If supervisor mode is implemented, bits mip.SSIP and **mie.SSIE** are the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for supervisor‑level software interrupts.  

- If the Sscofpmf extension is implemented, bits mip.LCOFIP and **mie.LCOFIE** are the interrupt‑pending and interrupt‑enable bits for local‑counter‑overflow interrupts.  

- If the Sscofpmf extension is not implemented, **mip.LCOFIP and mie.LCOFIE are read‑only zeros**.  

- If an interrupt is delegated to S‑mode by setting a bit in the mideleg register, it becomes visible in the sip register and is maskable using the sie register; otherwise, the corresponding bits in sip and **sie** are read‑only zero. (The sie register is the supervisor‑level view of **mie**.)

The following description:

- **MINH bit (bit 62) in minstretcfg** – "If set, then counting of events in M‑mode is inhibited."  
  *Condition:* MINH = 1 -> *Effect:* minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in M‑mode.

- **SINH bit (bit 61) in minstretcfg** – "If set, then counting of events in S/HS‑mode is inhibited."  
  *Condition:* SINH = 1 -> *Effect:* minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in S‑mode or HS‑mode.

- **UINH bit (bit 60) in minstretcfg** – "If set, then counting of events in U‑mode is inhibited."  
  *Condition:* UINH = 1 -> *Effect:* minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in U‑mode.

- **VSINH bit (bit 59) in minstretcfg** – "If set, then counting of events in VS‑mode is inhibited."  
  *Condition:* VSINH = 1 -> *Effect:* minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in VS‑mode.

- **VUINH bit (bit 58) in minstretcfg** – "If set, then counting of events in VU‑mode is inhibited."  
  *Condition:* VUINH = 1 -> *Effect:* minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in VU‑mode.

- **All x INH bits cleared** – "When all x INH bits are zero, event counting is enabled in all modes."  
  *Condition:* MINH = SINH = UINH = VSINH = VUINH = 0 -> *Effect:* minstret counter increments for instructions executed in any implemented privilege mode.

- **Unimplemented privilege modes** – "For each bit in 61:58, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit is read‑only zero."  
  *Condition:* Privilege mode not implemented -> *Effect:* Corresponding INH bit (SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH) reads as 0 and cannot be written.

- **RV32 access to high half** – "For RV32, bits 63:32 of minstretcfg can be accessed via the minstretcfgh CSR."  
  *Condition:* Architecture is RV32 -> *Effect:* minstretcfg[63:32] is read/writable through CSR minstretcfgh.

- **Supervisor‑level accessibility** – "The content of these registers may be accessible from Supervisor level if the Smcdeleg/Ssccfg extensions are implemented."  
  *Condition:* Smcdeleg and/or Ssccfg extensions are present -> *Effect:* Supervisor code can read/write minstretcfg (subject to the INH bits' rules).

- **Overflow (OF) bit** – "The bit position for the OF bit (bit 63) is read‑only 0, since these counters do not generate localcounter‑overflow interrupts on overflow."  
  *Condition:* Bit 63 (OF) -> *Effect:* Always reads as 0; no overflow interrupt is generated for minstret.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: If the MINH bit (bit 62) in the minstretcfg CSR is set to 1, the minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in M‑mode.  
RULE 2: If the SINH bit (bit 61) in the minstretcfg CSR is set to 1, the minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in S‑mode or HS‑mode.  
RULE 3: If the UINH bit (bit 60) in the minstretcfg CSR is set to 1, the minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in U‑mode.  
RULE 4: If the VSINH bit (bit 59) in the minstretcfg CSR is set to 1, the minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in VS‑mode.  
RULE 5: If the VUINH bit (bit 58) in the minstretcfg CSR is set to 1, the minstret counter does not increment for instructions executed in VU‑mode.  
RULE 6: When all INH bits (MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH) in the minstretcfg CSR are zero, the minstret counter increments for instructions executed in any implemented privilege mode.  
RULE 7: For each INH bit in positions 61 down to 58 of the minstretcfg CSR, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, the bit reads as 0 and is read‑only.  
RULE 8: On RV32 implementations, bits 63:32 of the minstretcfg CSR are accessed through the minstretcfgh CSR, allowing read and write of the high half of minstretcfg.  
RULE 9: If the Smcdeleg and/or Ssccfg extensions are implemented, supervisor‑mode code may read and write the minstretcfg CSR, subject to the INH‑bit behavior.  
RULE 10: The overflow (OF) bit at position 63 of the minstretcfg CSR is read‑only zero, and no local‑counter‑overflow interrupt is generated for the minstret counter.

The following description:

- **minstretcfg inhibition effect** – When `minstretcfg` is configured to inhibit a privilege mode, any instruction that retires while the CPU is in that inhibited mode does **not** increment the `instret` counter (and therefore does not increment the `minstret` register).  

- **Synchronous‑exception instructions** – Instructions that cause a synchronous exception to a more‑privileged mode are **not considered to retire** and **do not** increment `instret`/`minstret`.  

- **xRET instructions** – xRET instructions **do retire**, and **should** increment `instret`/`minstret` **only if the originating privilege mode is not inhibited** by `minstretcfg`.  

- **Illustrative scenario (minstretcfg inhibiting all modes except U‑mode)** – In this configuration:
  1. A user‑mode load that faults **does not** increment `instret`/`minstret` because the faulting execution does not retire.
  2. The exception‑handler instructions **do not** increment `instret`/`minstret` because they execute in an inhibited mode.
  3. The xRET that returns from the handler **does not** increment `instret`/`minstret` because it originates in an inhibited mode, even though it arguably retires in a non‑inhibited mode.
  4. Only when the load is re‑executed and successfully retires **does** it increment `instret`/`minstret`.  

- **Software emulation of inhibited instructions** – If an instruction is emulated by software running in a privilege mode that is inhibited by `minstretcfg`, the emulation routine **must** emulate the `instret` increment (and thus the `minstret` increment).  

- **Purpose of the definition** – The definition of `instret` (and by extension `minstret`) "is intended to ensure that the counter increments in a predictable fashion."
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: If minstretcfg is configured to inhibit a privilege mode, any instruction that retires while the CPU is executing in that inhibited mode must not increment minstret.  
RULE 2: Instructions that cause a synchronous exception to a more‑privileged mode are not considered to retire and must not increment minstret.  
RULE 3: xRET instructions retire and should increment minstret only when the originating privilege mode is not inhibited by minstretcfg.  
RULE 4: A load instruction that faults and therefore does not retire must not increment minstret.  
RULE 5: Instructions executed in a privilege mode that is inhibited by minstretcfg must not increment minstret.  
RULE 6: An xRET instruction that originates in a privilege mode inhibited by minstretcfg must not increment minstret even if it retires in a non‑inhibited mode.  
RULE 7: When a previously faulted load is re‑executed and successfully retires, it must increment minstret.  
RULE 8: If an instruction is emulated by software running in a privilege mode inhibited by minstretcfg, the emulation routine must increment minstret.  
RULE 9: The architectural definition of minstret is intended to ensure that the counter increments in a predictable fashion.

The following description:

- **Register definition** – The *mip* register is an **MXLEN‑bit read/write register** that contains information on pending interrupts. Bits 15:0 are allocated to standard interrupt causes only; bits 16 and above are designated for platform use.  

- **Interrupt trap condition** – An interrupt *i* will trap to M‑mode (causing the privilege mode to change to M‑mode) **if** bit *i* is set in both *mip* **and** *mie* (together with the other conditions on *mstatus* and *mideleg*).  

- **Evaluation timing** – The conditions for an interrupt trap to occur **must** be evaluated in a bounded amount of time from when an interrupt becomes, or ceases to be, pending in *mip*, and **must** also be evaluated immediately following the execution of an *xRET* instruction or an explicit write to a CSR on which these interrupt‑trap conditions expressly depend (including *mip*, *mie*, *mstatus*, and *mideleg*).  

- **Writable vs. read‑only bits** – Each individual bit in *mip* may be writable or may be read‑only.  
  - When bit *i* in *mip* is **writable**, a pending interrupt *i* **can be cleared** by writing 0 to this bit.  
  - If interrupt *i* can become pending but bit *i* in *mip* is **read‑only**, the implementation **must** provide some other mechanism for clearing the pending interrupt.  

- **Machine‑level external interrupt pending bit (MEIP)** – *mip*.MEIP **is read‑only**; it is set and cleared by a platform‑specific interrupt controller.  

- **Machine‑level timer interrupt pending bit (MTIP)** – *mip*.MTIP **is read‑only**; it **is cleared** by writing to the memory‑mapped machine‑mode timer compare register.  

- **Machine‑level software interrupt pending bit (MSIP)** – *mip*.MSIP **is read‑only**; it **is written** by accesses to memory‑mapped control registers that provide machine‑level interprocessor interrupts.  
  - A hart's memory‑mapped *msip* register is a 32‑bit read/write register, where bits 31‑1 read as zero and bit 0 contains the MSIP bit. When the memory‑mapped *msip* register changes, it **is guaranteed to be reflected in** *mip*.MSIP **eventually, but not necessarily immediately**.  
  - If a system has only one hart, or if a platform standard supports the delivery of machine‑level interprocessor interrupts through external interrupts (MEI) instead, then *mip*.MSIP and *mie*.MSIE **may both be read‑only zeros**.  

- **Supervisor‑mode not implemented** – If supervisor mode is **not implemented**, bits **SEIP**, **STIP**, and **SSIP** of *mip* (and the corresponding bits of *mie*) **are read‑only zeros**.  

- **Supervisor‑level external interrupt pending bit (SEIP)** – If supervisor mode **is implemented**:  
  - *mip*.SEIP **is writable** in *mip* and **may be written** by M‑mode software to indicate to S‑mode that an external interrupt is pending.  
  - The platform‑level interrupt controller **may generate** supervisor‑level external interrupts.  
  - Supervisor‑level external interrupts are **made pending** based on the logical‑OR of the software‑writable SEIP bit (**B**) and the signal (**E**) from the external interrupt controller.  
  - When *mip* is read with a CSR instruction, the value of the SEIP bit returned is **B || E**; the signal **E** **is not used** to calculate the value written to SEIP.  
  - Only the software‑writable SEIP bit participates in the read‑modify‑write sequence of a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction.  
  - **Example semantics**:  
    - For `csrrs t0, mip, t1`, `t0[9]` (the SEIP bit) is written with **B || E**, then **B** is written with **B || t1[9]**.  
    - For `csrrw t0, mip, t1`, `t0[9]` is written with **B || E**, and **B** is simply written with `t1[9]`. In neither case does **B** depend upon **E**.  

- **Supervisor‑level timer interrupt pending bit (STIP)** – If supervisor mode **is implemented**:  
  - If the *stimecmp* register **is not implemented**, *mip*.STIP **is writable** in *mip* and **may be written** by M‑mode software to deliver timer interrupts to S‑mode.  
  - If the *stimecmp* register **is implemented**, *mip*.STIP **is read‑only** in *mip* and **reflects** the supervisor‑level timer interrupt signal resulting from *stimecmp*. This timer interrupt signal **is cleared** by writing *stimecmp* with a value greater than the current time value.  

- **Supervisor‑level software interrupt pending bit (SSIP)** – If supervisor mode **is implemented**, *mip*.SSIP **is writable** in *mip* and **may also be set to 1** by a platform‑specific interrupt controller.  

- **Local‑counter‑overflow interrupt pending bit (LCOFIP)** – If the Sscofpmf extension **is implemented**, *mip*.LCOFIP **is read‑write** in *mip* and **reflects** the occurrence of a local counter‑overflow interrupt request resulting from any of the *mhpmevent* n.OF bits being set. If the Sscofpmf extension **is not implemented**, *mip*.LCOFIP **is a read‑only zero**.  

- **Priority handling of simultaneous M‑mode interrupts** – When multiple interrupts destined for M‑mode are pending in *mip*, they are handled in the following decreasing priority order: **MEI, MSI, MTI, SEI, SSI, STI, LCOFI**.  

- **Location of software‑interrupt bits** – Software‑interrupt pending bits are located in the lowest four bits of *mip*; this position **allows the use of a single CSR instruction with a five‑bit immediate** because these bits are often written by software.  

- **Restricted views (sip / sie)** – If an interrupt is delegated to S‑mode by setting a bit in *mideleg*, the corresponding bit **becomes visible in** the *sip* register and **is maskable using** the *sie* register; otherwise, the corresponding bits in *sip* and *sie* **are read‑only zero**.   (Only included because the visibility of *mip* bits influences their appearance in *sip*.)
============================================================

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: mip is an MXLEN‑bit read/write register that contains information on pending interrupts.  
RULE 2: Bits 15:0 of mip are allocated to standard interrupt causes only, and bits 16 and above are designated for platform use.  
RULE 3: An interrupt i traps to M‑mode if bit i is set in both mip and mie (together with the other conditions on mstatus and mideleg).  
RULE 4: The conditions for an interrupt trap must be evaluated in a bounded amount of time from when an interrupt becomes or ceases to be pending in mip.  
RULE 5: The conditions for an interrupt trap must be evaluated immediately after the execution of an xRET instruction or an explicit write to a CSR on which these conditions expressly depend, including mip.  
RULE 6: Each individual bit in mip may be either writable or read‑only.  
RULE 7: When a bit i in mip is writable, a pending interrupt i can be cleared by writing 0 to that bit.  
RULE 8: If an interrupt i can become pending but bit i in mip is read‑only, the implementation must provide some other mechanism for clearing the pending interrupt.  
RULE 9: mip.MEIP is read‑only and is set and cleared by a platform‑specific interrupt controller.  
RULE 10: mip.MTIP is read‑only and is cleared by writing to the memory‑mapped machine‑mode timer compare register.  
RULE 11: mip.MSIP is read‑only.  
RULE 12: mip.MSIP is written by accesses to memory‑mapped control registers that provide machine‑level interprocessor interrupts.  
RULE 13: The 32‑bit memory‑mapped msip register has bits 31‑1 read as zero and bit 0 containing the MSIP bit, and changes to this register are guaranteed to be eventually reflected in mip.MSIP but not necessarily immediately.  
RULE 14: If a system has only one hart, or if the platform standard delivers machine‑level interprocessor interrupts through external interrupts, then mip.MSIP and mie.MSIE may both be read‑only zeros.  
RULE 15: If supervisor mode is not implemented, the SEIP, STIP, and SSIP bits of mip are read‑only zeros.  
RULE 16: mip.SEIP is writable and may be written by M‑mode software to indicate to S‑mode that an external interrupt is pending.  
RULE 17: Supervisor‑level external interrupts become pending in mip based on the logical‑OR of the software‑writable SEIP bit and the external interrupt controller signal.  
RULE 18: When mip is read with a CSR instruction, the SEIP bit returned equals the logical‑OR of the software bit and the external signal, and the external signal is not used to calculate the value written to SEIP.  
RULE 19: Only the software‑writable SEIP bit participates in the read‑modify‑write sequence of a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction on mip.  
RULE 20: For a csrrs instruction to mip, the SEIP bit is first written with the logical‑OR of the software bit and the external signal, then the software bit is updated with the logical‑OR of its prior value and the source register bit.  
RULE 21: For a csrrw instruction to mip, the SEIP bit is first written with the logical‑OR of the software bit and the external signal, then the software bit is simply overwritten with the source register bit, and in neither case does the software bit depend on the external signal.  
RULE 22: If the stimecmp register is not implemented, mip.STIP is writable and may be written by M‑mode software to deliver timer interrupts to S‑mode.  
RULE 23: If the stimecmp register is implemented, mip.STIP is read‑only and reflects the supervisor‑level timer interrupt signal resulting from stimecmp, and this timer interrupt signal is cleared by writing stimecmp with a value greater than the current time value.  
RULE 24: mip.SSIP is writable and may also be set to 1 by a platform‑specific interrupt controller.  
RULE 25: If the Sscofpmf extension is implemented, mip.LCOFIP is read‑write and reflects the occurrence of a local counter‑overflow interrupt request resulting from any mhpmevent n.OF bits being set.  
RULE 26: If the Sscofpmf extension is not implemented, mip.LCOFIP is a read‑only zero.  
RULE 27: When multiple interrupts destined for M‑mode are pending in mip, they are handled in decreasing priority order: MEI, MSI, MTI, SEI, SSI, STI, LCOFI.  
RULE 28: Software‑interrupt pending bits are located in the lowest four bits of mip, allowing the use of a single CSR instruction with a five‑bit immediate because these bits are often written by software.  
RULE 29: If an interrupt is delegated to S‑mode by setting a bit in mideleg, the corresponding mip bit becomes visible in the sip register and is maskable using the sie register; otherwise the corresponding bits in sip and sie are read‑only zero.

RULE 3: When the associated OF bit becomes set, the LCOFIP bit in the mip register is eventually set, though the update need not occur immediately.  
RULE 4: Software clears the LCOFIP bit in the mip register before servicing a count‑overflow interrupt that resulted from one or more counter overflows.

The following description:

- The **misa CSR** is a **WARL read‑write register** reporting the ISA supported by the hart.  
- The **misa register must be readable in any implementation**, but a value of zero can be returned to indicate the misa register has not been implemented, requiring that CPU capabilities be determined through a separate non‑standard mechanism.  

**Register layout (Figure 2)**  

| Bits (MXLEN‑1 … 0) | Field                | Type   |
|--------------------|----------------------|--------|
| MXL[1:0]           | Machine XLEN (MXL)   | WARL   |
| –                  | 0                    | WARL   |
| Extensions[25:0]   | Extensions field     | WARL   |

- The **MXL (Machine XLEN) field** encodes the native base integer ISA width (Table 11). **The MXL field is read‑only.**  
- **If misa is nonzero, the MXL field indicates the effective XLEN in M‑mode**, a constant termed **MXLEN**. **XLEN is never greater than MXLEN**, but XLEN might be smaller than MXLEN in less‑privileged modes.  

**Table 11 – Encoding of MXL field in misa**

| MXL | XLEN |
|-----|------|
| 1   | 32   |
| 2   | 64   |
| 3   | Reserved |

- The **misa CSR is MXLEN bits wide**.  

- The **Extensions field** encodes the presence of the standard extensions, with a single bit per letter of the alphabet (bit 0 encodes "A", bit 1 encodes "B", …, bit 25 encodes "Z").  
- The **"I" bit will be set for the RV32I and RV64I base ISAs**, and the **"E" bit will be set for RV32E and RV64E**.  
- The Extensions field is a **WARL field that can contain writable bits where the implementation allows the supported ISA to be modified**.  
- **At reset, the Extensions field shall contain the maximal set of supported extensions, and "I" shall be selected over "E" if both are available.**  
- **When a standard extension is disabled by clearing its bit in misa, the instructions and CSRs defined or modified by the extension revert to their defined or reserved behaviors as if the extension is not implemented.**  
- Example: **setting misa.F=0 results in the F extension being not implemented for M‑mode, because the F extension's instructions will not act as the Unprivileged ISA requires but may instead raise an illegal‑instruction exception.**  

- **All bits that are reserved for future use must return zero when read.**  

**Table 12 – Encoding of Extensions field in misa**

| Bit | Character | Description                                              |
|-----|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| 0   | A         | Atomic extension                                         |
| 1   | B         | B extension                                              |
| 2   | C         | Compressed extension                                     |
| 3   | D         | Double‑precision floating‑point extension                |
| 4   | E         | RV32E/64E base ISA                                       |
| 5   | F         | Single‑precision floating‑point extension                |
| 6   | G         | Reserved                                                 |
| 7   | H         | Hypervisor extension                                     |
| 8   | I         | RV32I/64I base ISA                                       |
| 9   | J         | Reserved                                                 |
| 10  | K         | Reserved                                                 |
| 11  | L         | Reserved                                                 |
| 12  | M         | Integer Multiply/Divide extension                        |
| 13  | N         | Tentatively reserved for User‑Level Interrupts extension |
| 14  | O         | Reserved                                                 |
| 15  | P         | Tentatively reserved for Packed‑SIMD extension           |
| 16  | Q         | Quad‑precision floating‑point extension                  |
| 17  | R         | Reserved                                                 |
| 18  | S         | Supervisor mode implemented                              |
| 19  | T         | Reserved                                                 |
| 20  | U         | User mode implemented                                    |
| 21  | V         | Vector extension                                         |
| 22  | W         | Reserved                                                 |
| 23  | X         | Non‑standard extensions present                          |
| 24  | Y         | Reserved                                                 |
| 25  | Z         | Reserved                                                 |

- The **"X" bit will be set if there are any non‑standard extensions.**  

- **When the "B" bit is 1, the implementation supports the instructions provided by the Zba, Zbb, and Zbs extensions.**  
- **When the "B" bit is 0, it indicates that the implementation might not support one or more of the Zba, Zbb, or Zbs extensions.**  

- **When the "M" bit is 1, the implementation supports all multiply and division instructions defined by the M extension.**  
- **When the "M" bit is 0, it indicates that the implementation might not support those instructions.**  
- **However if the Zmmul extension is supported then the multiply instructions it specifies are supported irrespective of the value of the "M" bit.**  

- **When the "S" bit is 1, the implementation supports supervisor mode.**  
- **When the "S" bit is 0, the implementation might not support supervisor mode.**  

- **When the "U" bit is 1, the implementation supports user mode.**  
- **When the "U" bit is 0, the implementation might not support user mode.**  

- The **"E" bit is read‑only.**  
- **Unless misa is all read‑only zero, the "E" bit always reads as the complement of the "I" bit.**  
- **If an execution environment supports both RV32E and RV32I, software can select RV32E by clearing the "I" bit.**  

- **If an ISA feature x depends on an ISA feature y, then attempting to enable feature x but disable feature y results in both features being disabled.**  
  - Example: **setting "F"=0 and "D"=1 results in both "F" and "D" being cleared.**  
  - Example: **setting "U"=0 and "S"=1 results in both "U" and "S" being cleared.**  

- **An implementation may impose additional constraints on the collective setting of two or more misa fields, in which case they function collectively as a single WARL field.**  
- **An attempt to write an unsupported combination causes those bits to be set to some supported combination.**  

- **Writing misa may increase IALIGN, e.g., by disabling the "C" extension.**  
- **If an instruction that would write misa increases IALIGN, and the subsequent instruction's address is not IALIGN‑bit aligned, the write to misa is suppressed, leaving misa unchanged.**  

- **When software enables an extension that was previously disabled, then all state uniquely associated with that extension is UNSPECIFIED, unless otherwise specified by that extension.**  

- **Although one of the bits 25‑0 in misa being set to 1 implies that the corresponding feature is implemented, the inverse is not necessarily true: one of these bits being clear does not necessarily imply that the corresponding feature is not implemented.**
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================

RULE 2: The misa register must be readable in any implementation.

The following description:

- The **mscratch register** is an **MXLEN‑bit read/write register** dedicated for use by **machine mode**.

RULE 5: The operating system can rely on holding a value in mscratch while the user context is running.

The following description:

- **Register definition**  
  *mseccfg* is a 64‑bit read/write register that controls security features. It exists if any extension that adds a field to *mseccfg* is implemented; otherwise it is reserved.  

- **Fields added by the Zkr extension**  

  *SSEED* and *USEED* fields control access to the seed CSR from modes less privileged than M.  

  - When **USEED = 0**, access to the seed CSR in U‑mode raises an *illegal‑instruction* exception.  
  - When **USEED = 1**, read‑write access to the seed CSR from U‑mode is allowed; all other types of accesses raise an *illegal‑instruction* exception.  
  - If Zkr or U‑mode is not implemented, **USEED** is read‑only zero.  

  - When **SSEED = 0**, access to the seed CSR from S‑/HS‑mode raises an *illegal‑instruction* exception.  
  - When **SSEED = 1**, read‑write access to the seed CSR from S‑/HS‑mode is allowed; all other types of accesses raise an *illegal‑instruction* exception.  
  - If Zkr or S‑mode is not implemented, **SSEED** is read‑only zero.  

  - When the H extension is also implemented, access to the seed CSR from an HS‑qualified instruction leads to a *virtual‑instruction* exception in VS and VU modes; all other types of accesses raise an *illegal‑instruction* exception.  

- **Entropy Source Access Control (Table 20)**  

  | Mode | SSEED | USEED | Architectural effect |
  |------|-------|-------|-----------------------|
  | M    | –     | –     | The seed CSR is always available in machine mode as normal (with a CSR read‑write instruction). Attempted read without a write raises an *illegal‑instruction* exception regardless of mode and access control bits. |
  | U    | –     | 0     | Any seed CSR access raises an *illegal‑instruction* exception. |
  | U    | –     | 1     | The seed CSR is accessible as normal. No exception is raised for read‑write. |
  | S/HS | 0     | –     | Any seed CSR access raises an *illegal‑instruction* exception. |
  | S/HS | 1     | –     | The seed CSR is accessible as normal. No exception is raised for read‑write. |
  | VS/VU| 0     | –     | Any seed CSR access raises an *illegal‑instruction* exception. |
  | VS/VU| 1     | –     | A read‑write seed access raises a *virtual‑instruction* exception, while other access conditions raise an *illegal‑instruction* exception. |

- **Fields added by the Smepmp extension**  

  - **RLB (Rule Locking Bypass)** – a WARL field.  
    * When **mseccfg.RLB = 1**, locked PMP rules may be removed or modified and locked PMP rules may be edited.  
    * When **mseccfg.RLB = 0** and **pmpcfg.L = 1** in any rule or entry (including disabled entries), then **mseccfg.RLB** remains 0 and any further modifications to **mseccfg.RLB** are ignored until a PMP reset.  

  - **MMWP (Machine‑Mode Allowlist Policy)** – a WARL field, sticky (cannot be cleared until a PMP reset).  
    * When **mseccfg.MMWP** is set, the default PMP policy for Machine mode when accessing memory regions that do not have a matching PMP rule changes to *denied* instead of *ignored*.  

  - **MML (Machine Mode Lockdown)** – a WARL field, sticky (cannot be cleared until a PMP reset).  
    *When **mseccfg.MML** is set, the system's behavior changes as follows:*  

    1. **Interpretation of pmpcfg.L** changes:  
       - Instead of marking a rule as locked and enforced in all modes, **pmpcfg.L** now marks a rule as **M‑mode‑only** when set and **S/U‑mode‑only** when unset.  
       - The formerly reserved encoding **pmpcfg.RW = 01**, and the encoding **pmpcfg.LRWX = 1111**, now encode a **Shared‑Region**.  

    2. **Enforcement of the new rule types**  
       - An **M‑mode‑only rule** is enforced on Machine mode and denied in Supervisor or User mode. It also remains locked so that any further modifications to its associated configuration or address registers are ignored until a PMP reset, unless **mseccfg.RLB** is set.  
       - An **S/U‑mode‑only rule** is enforced on Supervisor and User modes and denied on Machine mode.  
       - A **Shared‑Region rule** where **pmpcfg.L is not set** can be used for sharing data between M‑mode and S/U‑mode; it is not executable. M‑mode has read/write access; S/U‑mode has read access if **pmpcfg.X** is not set, or read/write access if **pmpcfg.X** is set.  
       - A **Shared‑Region rule** where **pmpcfg.L is set** can be used for sharing code between M‑mode and S/U‑mode; it is not writable. Both M‑mode and S/U‑mode have execute access; M‑mode also has read access if **pmpcfg.X** is set. The rule remains locked so that any further modifications to its associated configuration or address registers are ignored until a PMP reset, unless **mseccfg.RLB** is set.  
       - The encoding **pmpcfg.LRWX = 1111** can be used for sharing data between M‑mode and S/U‑mode, where both modes only have read‑only access. The rule remains locked so that any further modifications to its associated configuration or address registers are ignored until a PMP reset, unless **mseccfg.RLB** is set.  

    3. **Restrictions on PMP rule writes**  
       - Adding a rule with executable privileges that either is **M‑mode‑only** or a locked **Shared‑Region** is not possible; such **pmpcfg** writes are ignored, leaving **pmpcfg** unchanged. This restriction can be temporarily lifted by setting **mseccfg.RLB**.  

    4. **Code execution**  
       - Executing code with Machine mode privileges is only possible from memory regions with a matching **M‑mode‑only rule** or a locked **Shared‑Region rule** with executable privileges. Executing code from a region without a matching rule or with a matching **S/U‑mode‑only rule** is denied.  

    5. **When MML is not set**  
       - If **mseccfg.MML** is not set, the combination **pmpcfg.RW = 01** remains reserved for future standard use.  

- **Fields added by the Smmpm extension**  

  - **PMM** field enables or disables pointer masking for M‑mode.  
    * If Smmpm is not implemented, **PMM** is read‑only zero.  
    * **PMM** is read‑only zero for RV32.  

  **Legal values of the PMM WARL field (Table 21):**  

  | Value | Description |
  |------|-------------|
  | 00   | Pointer masking is disabled (PMLEN = 0) |
  | 01   | Reserved |
  | 10   | Pointer masking is enabled with PMLEN = XLEN − 57 (PMLEN = 7 on RV64) |
  | 11   | Pointer masking is enabled with PMLEN = XLEN − 48 (PMLEN = 16 on RV64) |

- **Field added by the Zicfilp extension**  

  - **MLPE** field in *mseccfg*.  
    * When **MLPE = 1**, the Zicfilp extension is enabled in M‑mode.  
    * When **MLPE = 0**, the Zicfilp extension is not enabled in M‑mode and the following rules apply to M‑mode:  
      - The hart does not update the ELP state; it remains as **NO_LP_EXPECTED**.  
      - The **LPAD** instruction operates as a no‑op.  

- **Alias register for XLEN=32**  

  - When XLEN = 32 only, **mseccfgh** is a 32‑bit read/write register that aliases bits 63:32 of *mseccfg*. **mseccfgh** exists when XLEN = 32 and *mseccfg* is implemented; it does not exist when XLEN = 64.

The following description:

- For RV64 harts, the Smstateen extension adds four new 64‑bit CSRs at machine level: **mstateen0 (Machine State Enable 0), mstateen1, mstateen2, and mstateen3**.  

- **Each bit of a stateen CSR controls less‑privileged access to an extension's state**. (Applies to mstateen0.)  

- **The stateen registers at each level control access to state at all less‑privileged levels, but not at its own level**. (Thus mstateen0 controls access to state for supervisor‑mode and user‑mode, but not for machine‑mode.)  

- **When a stateen CSR prevents access to state by less‑privileged levels, an attempt in one of those privilege modes to execute an instruction that would read or write the protected state raises an illegal‑instruction exception, or, if executing in VS or VU mode and the circumstances for a virtual‑instruction exception apply, raises a virtual‑instruction exception instead of an illegal‑instruction exception**. (mstateen0 can cause such exceptions for accesses from S‑mode, U‑mode, VS, or VU.)  

- **For every bit with a defined purpose in an sstateen CSR, the same bit is defined in the matching mstateen CSR to control access below machine level to the same state**. (Therefore each bit of sstateen0 has a corresponding bit in mstateen0.)  

- **The upper 32 bits of an mstateen CSR (or for RV32, the corresponding high‑half CSR) control access to state that is inherently inaccessible to user level, so no corresponding enable bits in the supervisor‑level sstateen CSR are applicable**. (Bits 63‑32 of mstateen0 have this property.)  

- **Each standard‑defined bit of a stateen CSR is WARL and may be read‑only zero or one, subject to the following conditions**:  

  * **Bits in any stateen CSR that are defined to control state that a hart doesn't implement are read‑only zeros for that hart**.  

  * **All reserved bits not yet given a defined meaning are also read‑only zeros**.  

  * **For every bit in an mstateen CSR that is zero (whether read‑only zero or set to zero), the same bit appears as read‑only zero in the matching hstateen and sstateen CSRs**. (Thus a zero bit in mstateen0 forces the corresponding bit in hstateen0 and sstateen0 to be read‑only zero.)  

  * **For every bit in an hstateen CSR that is zero (whether read‑only zero or set to zero), the same bit appears as read‑only zero in sstateen when accessed in VS‑mode**.

- **For each mstateen CSR, bit 63 is defined to control access to the matching sstateen and hstateen CSRs. That is, bit 63 of mstateen0 controls access to sstateen0 and hstateen0**.  

- **Bit 63 of each hstateen CSR correspondingly controls access to the matching sstateen CSR**.  

- **Bit 63 of each mstateen CSR may be read‑only zero only if the hypervisor extension is not implemented and the matching supervisor‑level sstateen CSR is all read‑only zeros. - "The stateen registers at each level control access to state at all less‑privileged levels, but not at its own level.  Just as with the counteren CSRs, when a stateen CSR prevents access to state by less‑privileged levels, an attempt in one of those privilege modes to execute an instruction that would read or write the protected state raises an illegal‑instruction exception, or, if executing in VS or VU mode and the circumstances for a virtual‑instruction exception apply, raises a virtual‑instruction exception instead of an illegal‑instruction exception."  (Applies to **mstateen1**.)

- "When a stateen CSR prevents access to state for a privilege mode, attempting to execute in that privilege mode an instruction that implicitly updates the state without reading it may or may not raise an illegal‑instruction or virtual‑instruction exception.  Such cases must be disambiguated by being explicitly specified one way or the other."  (Applies to **mstateen1**.)

- "For every bit with a defined purpose in an sstateen CSR, the same bit is defined in the matching mstateen CSR to control access below machine level to the same state."  (Thus each defined bit in **sstateen1** has a counterpart in **mstateen1**.)

- "The upper 32 bits of an mstateen CSR (or for RV32, the corresponding high‑half CSR) control access to state that is inherently inaccessible to user level, so no corresponding enable bits in the supervisor‑level sstateen CSR are applicable."  (Therefore bits 63‑32 of **mstateen1** have this property.)

- "Bits in any stateen CSR that are defined to control state that a hart doesn't implement are read‑only zeros for that hart.  Likewise, all reserved bits not yet given a defined meaning are also read‑only zeros.  For every bit in an mstateen CSR that is zero (whether read‑only zero or set to zero), the same bit appears as readonly zero in the matching hstateen and sstateen CSRs."  (Governs zero‑read‑only bits of **mstateen1**.)

- "On reset, all writable mstateen bits are initialized by the hardware to zeros."  (Thus all writable bits of **mstateen1** are zero after reset.)

- "If machine‑level software changes these values, it is responsible for initializing the corresponding writable bits of the hstateen and sstateen CSRs to zeros too."  (If software writes **mstateen1**, it must also zero the matching bits in **hstateen1** and **sstateen1**.)

- "For each mstateen CSR, bit 63 is defined to control access to the matching sstateen and hstateen CSRs.  That is, … bit 63 of **mstateen1** controls access to **sstateen1** and **hstateen1**; etc."  

- "Bit 63 of each mstateen CSR may be read‑only zero only if the hypervisor extension is not implemented and the matching supervisor‑level sstateen CSR is all read‑only zeros.  In that case, machine‑level software should emulate attempts to access the affected sstateen CSR from S‑mode, ignoring writes and returning zero for reads."  (Thus **bit 63 of mstateen1** may be read‑only zero under that condition, and the described emulation behavior applies.)

- For RV64 harts, this extension adds four new 64‑bit CSRs at machine level: **mstateen0 (Machine State Enable 0), mstateen1, mstateen2, and mstateen3**.

(Thus each bit of mstateen2 controls less‑privileged access to the corresponding extension state.)

The following description:

- For RV64 harts the Smstateen extension **adds a 64‑bit CSR named mstateen3** at machine level.  

- For RV32 harts there is a CSR address **mstateen3h** that provides access to the upper 32 bits of the corresponding machine‑level mstateen3 register.  

- **Each bit of a stateen CSR controls less‑privileged access to an extension's state.** Consequently, every bit in mstateen3 controls whether software in a less‑privileged mode (S‑mode, U‑mode, VS‑mode, VU‑mode) may read or write the corresponding piece of extension state.  

- **The stateen registers at each level control access to state at all less‑privileged levels, but not at their own level.** Thus mstateen3 does **not** restrict machine‑mode accesses, only accesses from lower privilege modes.  

- **When a stateen CSR prevents access to state for a privilege mode, an attempt in that privilege mode to execute an instruction that would read or write the protected state raises an illegal‑instruction exception, or, if executing in VS‑ or VU‑mode and the circumstances for a virtual‑instruction exception apply, raises a virtual‑instruction exception instead of an illegal‑instruction exception.** (Applies to mstateen3.)  

- **When a stateen CSR prevents access to state for a privilege mode, attempting to execute in that privilege mode an instruction that implicitly updates the state without reading it may or may not raise an illegal‑instruction or virtual‑instruction exception.  Such cases must be disambiguated by being explicitly specified one way or the other.** (Applies to mstateen3.)  

- **For every bit with a defined purpose in an sstateen CSR, the same bit is defined in the matching mstateen CSR to control access below machine level to the same state.** Hence each defined bit in sstateen3 has a counterpart in mstateen3 that governs the same piece of state for lower privilege modes.  

- **Bit 63 of each mstateen CSR is defined to control access to the matching sstateen and hstateen CSRs.** Therefore **bit 63 of mstateen3 controls access to sstateen3 and hstateen3.**  

- **Bit 63 of each mstateen CSR may be read‑only zero only if the hypervisor extension is not implemented and the matching supervisor‑level sstateen CSR is all read‑only zeros.** In that case, machine‑level software should emulate attempts to access the affected sstateen CSR from S‑mode, ignoring writes and returning zero for reads.  

- **On reset, all writable mstateen bits are initialized by the hardware to zeros.** Consequently, after reset every writable bit in mstateen3 is zero.  

- **Each standard‑defined bit of a stateen CSR is WARL and may be read‑only zero or one, subject to the following conditions:**  
  - **Bits that are defined to control state that a hart does not implement are read‑only zeros for that hart.**  
  - **All reserved bits not yet given a defined meaning are also read‑only zeros.**  

- **For every bit in an mstateen CSR that is zero (whether read‑only zero or set to zero), the same bit appears as read‑only zero in the matching hstateen and sstateen CSRs.** Thus any zero bit in mstateen3 forces the corresponding bits in sstateen3 and hstateen3 to be read‑only zero.  

- **A bit in a supervisor‑level sstateen CSR cannot be read‑only one unless the same bit is read‑only one in the matching mstateen CSR (and, if it exists, in the matching hstateen CSR).** Therefore a read‑only‑one bit in sstateen3 requires the corresponding bit in mstateen3 to be read‑only one.  

- **A bit in an hstateen CSR cannot be read‑only one unless the same bit is read‑only one in the matching mstateen CSR.** Hence a read‑only‑one bit in hstateen3 requires the corresponding bit in mstateen3 to be read‑only one.  

- **With the hypervisor extension, the hstateen CSRs have identical encodings to the mstateen CSRs, except they control accesses for a virtual machine (from VS and VU modes).** Consequently, the encoding of mstateen3 is identical to that of hstateen3.  

- **Each bit of a stateen CSR may have a dual purpose as an enable for the ISA extension that introduces the controlled state.** Therefore individual bits in mstateen3 can also serve as enables for the corresponding ISA extensions.

The following description:

- mstatus includes a vector context status field **VS** located in bits **mstatus[10:9]**; the same bits are **shadowed in sstatus[10:9]**.  
- The VS field is defined **analogously to the floating‑point context status field FS**.  

**Illegal‑instruction exception**  
- **Condition:** mstatus.VS = **Off** and an attempt is made to **execute any vector instruction** or to **access any vector CSR**.  
- **Effect:** an **illegal‑instruction exception** is raised.  

**Transition to Dirty**  
- **Condition:** mstatus.VS = **Initial** or **Clean** and an **instruction that changes vector state** is executed (including accesses to vector CSRs).  
- **Effect:** mstatus.VS is changed to **Dirty**.  

- **Condition:** mstatus.VS = **Initial** or **Clean**.  
- **Effect:** an implementation **may** change mstatus.VS to **Dirty** at any time, even when there is no change in vector state.  

**Interaction with mstatus.SD**  
- **Condition:** mstatus.VS = **Dirty**.  
- **Effect:** mstatus.SD is set to **1**.  

- **Condition:** mstatus.VS ≠ **Dirty**.  
- **Effect:** mstatus.SD is set **in accordance with existing specifications** (i.e., the prior rule for SD applies).  

**Existence of VS relative to misa.V**  
- Implementations **may** have a **writable misa.V field**.  
- **Condition:** misa.V is **clear**.  
- **Effect:** the mstatus.VS field **may** still exist.  

- Allowing mstatus.VS to exist when misa.V is clear **enables vector emulation** and **simplifies handling of mstatus.VS** in systems with a writable misa.V (descriptive statement).
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The mstatus register includes a vector context status field VS located in bits mstatus[10:9], and the same bits are shadowed in sstatus[10:9].  
RULE 2: The VS field in mstatus is defined analogously to the floating‑point context status field FS.  
RULE 3: If mstatus.VS equals Off and an attempt is made to execute any vector instruction or to access any vector CSR, an illegal‑instruction exception is raised.  
RULE 4: If mstatus.VS equals Initial or Clean and an instruction that changes vector state is executed (including accesses to vector CSRs), then mstatus.VS is changed to Dirty.  
RULE 5: When mstatus.VS equals Initial or Clean, an implementation may change mstatus.VS to Dirty at any time, even when there is no change in vector state.  
RULE 6: If mstatus.VS equals Dirty, then mstatus.SD is set to 1.  
RULE 7: If mstatus.VS does not equal Dirty, then mstatus.SD is set in accordance with existing specifications.  
RULE 8: If the misa.V field is clear, the mstatus.VS field may still exist.  
RULE 9: Allowing mstatus.VS to exist when misa.V is clear enables vector emulation and simplifies handling of mstatus.VS in systems with a writable misa.V.

The following description:

- The global interrupt‑enable bits **MIE** and **SIE** are located in the low‑order bits of **mstatus**, allowing them to be atomically set or cleared with a single CSR instruction.  

- When a hart is executing in privilege mode **x**, interrupts are globally enabled when **xIE = 1** and globally disabled when **xIE = 0**.  

- Interrupts for lower‑privilege modes (**w < x**) are always globally disabled regardless of the setting of any global **wIE** bit for the lower‑privilege mode.  

- Interrupts for higher‑privilege modes (**y > x**) are always globally enabled regardless of the setting of the global **yIE** bit for the higher‑privilege mode.  

- If supervisor mode is not implemented, then **SIE** and **SPIE** are read‑only **0**.  

- Each privilege mode **x** that can respond to interrupts has a two‑level stack of interrupt‑enable bits and privilege modes. **xPIE** holds the value of the interrupt‑enable bit active prior to the trap, and **xPP** holds the previous privilege mode.  

- The **xPP** fields can only hold privilege modes up to **x**, so **MPP** is two bits wide and **SPP** is one bit wide.  

- When a trap is taken from privilege mode **y** into privilege mode **x**:  
  * **xPIE** is set to the value of **xIE**;  
  * **xIE** is set to **0**;  
  * **xPP** is set to **y**.  

- An **MRET** or **SRET** instruction returns from a trap in M‑mode or S‑mode respectively. When executing an **xRET** instruction, supposing **xPP** holds the value **y**:  
  * **xIE** is set to **xPIE**;  
  * the privilege mode is changed to **y**;  
  * **xPIE** is set to **1**;  
  * **xPP** is set to the least‑privileged supported mode (U if U‑mode is implemented, else M);  
  * If **y ≠ M**, **xRET** also sets **MPRV = 0**.  

- Setting **xPP** to the least‑privileged supported mode on an **xRET** helps identify software bugs in the management of the two‑level privilege‑mode stack.  

- **xPP** fields are WARL fields that can hold only privilege mode **x** and any implemented privilege mode lower than **x**. If privilege mode **x** is not implemented, then **xPP** **must be read‑only 0**.  

- **M‑mode** software can determine whether a privilege mode is implemented by writing that mode to **MPP** then reading it back.  

- If the machine provides only U and M modes, then only a single hardware storage bit is required to represent either **00** or **11** in **MPP**.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The global interrupt‑enable bits MIE and SIE reside in the low‑order bits of mstatus, permitting atomic set or clear with a single CSR instruction.  
RULE 2: In mstatus, when a hart is executing in privilege mode x, the xIE bit being 1 globally enables interrupts for that mode and the xIE bit being 0 globally disables interrupts for that mode.  
RULE 3: In mstatus, interrupt enable for any lower‑privilege mode w (w < x) is always globally disabled irrespective of the value of the wIE bit.  
RULE 4: In mstatus, interrupt enable for any higher‑privilege mode y (y > x) is always globally enabled irrespective of the value of the yIE bit.  
RULE 5: If supervisor mode is not implemented, the SIE and SPIE fields of mstatus are read‑only 0.  
RULE 6: For each privilege mode x that can respond to interrupts, the mstatus field xPIE stores the interrupt‑enable bit value that was active prior to a trap, and the mstatus field xPP stores the previous privilege mode.  
RULE 7: The xPP fields in mstatus can hold only privilege modes up to x, resulting in MPP being two bits wide and SPP being one bit wide.  
RULE 8: When a trap is taken from privilege mode y into privilege mode x, the mstatus field xPIE is set to the current value of xIE, the mstatus field xIE is cleared to 0, and the mstatus field xPP is written with y.  
RULE 9: Executing an xRET instruction (MRET or SRET) sets the mstatus field xIE to the value of xPIE, changes the current privilege mode to the value stored in xPP, sets xPIE in mstatus to 1, writes xPP in mstatus with the least‑privileged supported mode (U if U‑mode is implemented, otherwise M), and, if the saved privilege mode y is not M, also clears the MPRV bit in mstatus.  
RULE 10: Setting the xPP field in mstatus to the least‑privileged supported mode on an xRET is intended to aid detection of software bugs in the two‑level privilege‑mode stack management.  
RULE 11: The xPP fields in mstatus are WARL fields that may contain only privilege mode x or any implemented privilege mode lower than x, and if privilege mode x is not implemented, the xPP field must be read‑only 0.  
RULE 12: M‑mode software can determine whether a privilege mode is implemented by writing that mode to the MPP field of mstatus and then reading it back.  
RULE 13: When a machine implements only U and M privilege modes, a single hardware storage bit in the mstatus MPP field suffices to represent either the binary pattern 00 or 11.

The following description:

- The M-mode-disable-trap (MDT) bit is a WARL field introduced by the Smdbltrp extension.  
- Upon reset, the MDT field is set to 1.  
- When the MDT bit is set to 1 by an explicit CSR write, the MIE (Machine Interrupt Enable) bit is cleared to 0.  
- For RV64, this clearing occurs regardless of the value written, if any, to the MIE bit by the same write.  
- The MIE bit can only be set to 1 by an explicit CSR write if the MDT bit is already 0 or, for RV64, is being set to 0 by the same write.  
- For RV32, the MDT bit is in mstatush and the MIE bit in mstatus register.  
- When a trap is to be taken into M-mode, if the MDT bit is currently 0, it is then set to 1, and the trap is delivered as expected.  
- However, if MDT is already set to 1, then this is an unexpected trap.  
- When the Smrnmi extension is implemented, a trap caused by an RNMI is not considered an unexpected trap irrespective of the state of the MDT bit.  
- A trap caused by an RNMI does not set the MDT bit.  
- A trap that occurs when executing in M-mode with mnstatus.NMIE set to 0 is an unexpected trap.  
- The MRET and SRET instructions, when executed in M-mode, set the MDT bit to 0.  
- If the new privilege mode is U, VS, or VU, then sstatus.SDT is also set to 0.  
- Additionally, if it is VU, then vsstatus.SDT is also set to 0.  
- The MNRET instruction, provided by the Smrnmi extension, sets the MDT bit to 0 if the new privilege mode is not M.  
- If it is U, VS, or VU, then sstatus.SDT is also set to 0.  
- Additionally, if it is VU, then vsstatus.SDT is also set to 0.

=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: The MDT bit in mstatus is a WARL field introduced by the Smdbltrp extension.  
RULE 2: Upon reset, the MDT field in mstatus is set to 1.  
RULE 3: When the MDT bit in mstatus is set to 1 by an explicit CSR write, the MIE bit in mstatus is cleared to 0.  
RULE 4: On RV64, the clearing of the MIE bit in mstatus to 0 occurs regardless of the value written, if any, to the MIE bit by the same CSR write that sets the MDT bit to 1.  
RULE 5: The MIE bit in mstatus may be set to 1 by an explicit CSR write only if the MDT bit in mstatus is already 0, or, on RV64, if the MDT bit is being set to 0 by the same write.  
RULE 6: On RV32, the MDT bit resides in mstatush while the MIE bit resides in the mstatus register.  
RULE 7: When a trap is taken into M-mode and the MDT bit in mstatus is currently 0, the MDT bit is set to 1 and the trap is delivered as expected.  
RULE 8: If the MDT bit in mstatus is already 1 when a trap is taken into M-mode, the trap is considered unexpected.  
RULE 9: When the Smrnmi extension is implemented, a trap caused by an RNMI is not considered unexpected regardless of the MDT bit state in mstatus.  
RULE 10: A trap caused by an RNMI does not set the MDT bit in mstatus.  
RULE 11: When executed in M-mode, the MRET instruction sets the MDT bit in mstatus to 0.

The following description:

- For RV64 harts, the **SXL** and **UXL** fields are **WARL** fields that control the value of XLEN for **S‑mode** and **U‑mode**, respectively.  

- The encoding of the **SXL** and **UXL** fields is the same as the **MXL** field of **misa**, shown in Table 11.  

- **When MXLEN = 32**, the **SXL** and **UXL** fields do not exist, and **SXLEN = 32** and **UXLEN = 32**.  

- **When MXLEN = 64**, if **S‑mode is not supported**, then **SXL** is **read‑only zero**.  

- **When MXLEN = 64**, if **S‑mode is supported**, then **SXL** is a **WARL** field that encodes the current value of **SXLEN**.  

- **In particular, an implementation may make SXL be a read‑only field whose value always ensures that SXLEN = MXLEN**.  

- **When MXLEN = 64**, if **U‑mode is not supported**, then **UXL** is **read‑only zero**.  

- **When MXLEN = 64**, if **U‑mode is supported**, then **UXL** is a **WARL** field that encodes the current value of **UXLEN**.  

- **In particular, an implementation may make UXL be a read‑only field whose value always ensures that UXLEN = MXLEN or UXLEN = SXLEN**.  

- **If S‑mode is implemented**, the set of legal values that the **UXL** field may assume **excludes those that would cause UXLEN to be greater than SXLEN**.  

- **Whenever XLEN in any mode is set to a value less than the widest supported XLEN**, all operations **must ignore source operand register bits above the configured XLEN**, and **must sign‑extend results to fill the entire widest supported XLEN in the destination register**.  

- **Similarly, pc bits above XLEN are ignored, and when the pc is written, it is sign‑extended to fill the widest supported XLEN**.  

- **We require that operations always fill the entire underlying hardware registers with defined values to avoid implementation‑defined behavior**.  

- **To reduce hardware complexity, the architecture imposes no checks that lower‑privilege modes have XLEN settings less than or equal to the next‑higher privilege mode**.  

- **In practice, such settings would almost always be a software bug, but machine operation is well‑defined even in this case**.  

- **When such a HINT is executed with XLEN < MXLEN and bits MXLEN..XLEN of the destination register not all equal to bit XLEN‑1, it is implementation‑defined whether bits MXLEN..XLEN of the destination register are unchanged or are overwritten with copies of bit XLEN‑1**.  

- **The implementation choice is observable only by privilege modes with an XLEN setting greater than the current XLEN; it is invisible to the current privilege mode**.
============================================================
