- **Address encoding (RV32)** – *Each PMP address register encodes bits 33‑2 of a 34‑bit physical address for RV32.* Thus, when the hart implements RV32, pmpaddr12 holds bits 33‑2 of the physical address associated with PMP entry 12.  

- **Address encoding (RV64)** – *For RV64, each PMP address register encodes bits 55‑2 of a 56‑bit physical address.* Thus, when the hart implements RV64, pmpaddr12 holds bits 55‑2 of the physical address associated with PMP entry 12.  

- **WARL property** – *All PMP CSR fields are WARL and may be read‑only zero.* Therefore the value read from pmpaddr12 is **Write‑Any‑Read‑Legal (WARL)**: any written value that conforms to the implementation's supported address bits is legal, and implementations may force the register to read as zero.  

- **Partial physical‑address support** – *Not all physical address bits may be implemented, and so the pmpaddr registers are WARL.* Consequently, if the implementation does not support the full range of bits 33‑2 (RV32) or 55‑2 (RV64), the corresponding high‑order bits of pmpaddr12 are treated as WARL.  

- **Relation to PMP entry description** – *PMP entries are described by an 8‑bit configuration register and one MXLEN‑bit address register.* Hence pmpaddr12 supplies the address portion for PMP entry 12, paired with its 8‑bit configuration register (pmp12cfg).

  | y011…1111            | NAPOT          | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range |
  | 0111…1111            | NAPOT          | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
  | 1111…1111            | NAPOT          | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

  (The pattern "yyyy…yyyy" denotes the bits of pmpaddr13; the table applies identically to pmpaddr13.)

- **TOR address‑matching mode**  
  * If pmpcfg13.A = TOR, pmpaddr13 forms the **top** of the address range for PMP entry 13.  
  * The address range matched by entry 13 is any address y such that  

    `pmpaddr12 ≤ y < pmpaddr13`  

    (the lower bound uses the preceding PMP address register, pmpaddr12, irrespective of pmpcfg12.)

  * If `pmpaddr12 ≥ pmpaddr13` and `pmpcfg13.A = TOR`, then PMP entry 13 matches **no** addresses.

- **Effect of PMP granularity G on bits of pmpaddr13**  

  *When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg13.A[1] is set (i.e., the mode is NAPOT):*  
    - Bits `pmpaddr13[G‑2:0]` **read as all ones**.  

  *When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg13.A[1] is clear (i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR):*  
    - Bits `pmpaddr13[G‑1:0]` **read as all zeros**.

The following description:

- **pmpaddr15 is a PMP address register.**  
  The PMP address registers are CSRs named *pmpaddr0‑pmpaddr63*; therefore *pmpaddr15* is one of these registers.

- **WARL property.**  
  *All PMP CSR fields are WARL and may be read‑only zero.* Hence the value in *pmpaddr15* is WARL and may be hard‑wired to zero.

- **Encoded address bits (RV32).**  
  *Each PMP address register encodes bits 33‑2 of a 34‑bit physical address for RV32.* Thus *pmpaddr15* holds bits 33‑2 of the physical address used by PMP entry 15 when the hart implements RV32.

- **Encoded address bits (RV64).**  
  *For RV64, each PMP address register encodes bits 55‑2 of a 56‑bit physical address.* Therefore *pmpaddr15* holds bits 55‑2 of the physical address used by PMP entry 15 when the hart implements RV64.

- **Implementation‑dependent physical‑address bits.**  
  *Not all physical address bits may be implemented, and so the pmpaddr registers are WARL.* Consequently, the subset of bits actually implemented in *pmpaddr15* depends on the implementation.

- **Use as preceding address register.**  
  *Some PMP settings additionally use the address register associated with the preceding PMP entry.* Accordingly, *pmpaddr15* may be used as the preceding address register for PMP entry 16 (if entry 16 exists).

- **Existence depends on number of PMP entries implemented.**  
  *Implementations may implement zero, 16, or 64 PMP entries; the lowest‑numbered PMP entries must be implemented first.* Hence *pmpaddr15* is present only in implementations that support at least 16 PMP entries.

The following description:

- **NAPOT range encoding (Table 24)** – For any PMP address register, including pmpaddr16, the low‑order bits of the register encode the size of a NAPOT range as follows:  

  • If pmpcfg.A = NA4, then a value of the form `yyyy…yyyy` in pmpaddr16 matches a **4‑byte NAPOT range**.  

  • If pmpcfg.A = NAPOT and the low bits of pmpaddr16 are `…yyy0`, the register matches an **8‑byte NAPOT range**.  

  • If pmpcfg.A = NAPOT and the low bits of pmpaddr16 are `…yy01`, the register matches a **16‑byte NAPOT range**.  

  • If pmpcfg.A = NAPOT and the low bits of pmpaddr16 are `…y011`, the register matches a **32‑byte NAPOT range**.  

  • … (subsequent patterns continue as shown in Table 24, ending with `1111…1111` matching a **2·XLEN + 3‑byte NAPOT range**).

- **TOR address‑matching (Section 3.7.1.1)** – When the configuration field pmpcfg for entry i is set to **TOR**, the associated address register (e.g., pmpaddr16 when i = 16) forms the **top** of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the **bottom** of the range.  

  • If pmpcfg_i.A = TOR, the entry matches any address y such that pmpaddr_{i‑1} ≤ y < pmpaddr_i (irrespective of pmpcfg_{i‑1}).  

  • If i = 0 and pmpcfg_0.A = TOR, the lower bound is zero, so the entry matches any address y < pmpaddr0.  

  • If pmpaddr_{i‑1} ≥ pmpaddr_i and pmpcfg_i.A = TOR, then the entry matches **no** addresses.

- **Effect of PMP granularity G on the value read from pmpaddr16** (Section 3.7.1.1, granularity discussion):  

  • When G ≥ 2 **and** pmpcfg_i.A[1] = 1 (i.e., the mode is NAPOT), **bits pmpaddr_i[G‑2:0] read as all ones**.  

  • When G ≥ 1 **and** pmpcfg_i.A[1] = 0 (i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR), **bits pmpaddr_i[G‑1:0] read as all zeros**.  

  • **Bits pmpaddr_i[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic**.  

  • Changing pmpcfg_i.A[1] **affects the value read from pmpaddr_i** but **does not affect the underlying stored value**; specifically, **pmpaddr_i[G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg_i.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF and then back to NAPOT**.

- **Granularity limitation on NA4 mode** – When G ≥ 1, the **NA4 mode is not selectable** for any PMP entry, including the entry that uses pmpaddr16.
============================================================

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: If pmpcfg.A = NA4, then a value of the form yyyy…yyyy in pmpaddr16 matches a 4‑byte NAPOT range.

The following description:

- **Read‑modify‑write of pmpaddr19 with CSRRS or CSRRC**  
  *Condition:* An executing **CSRRS** or **CSRRC** instruction accesses the CSR **pmpaddr19**, and the rs1 register contains a bit mask that does **not** set the bit position corresponding to **pmpaddr19[G‑1]**.  
  *Effect:* Because **pmpaddr19[G‑1]** may have an underlying value of 1 but read as 0, the instruction will read **0** from **pmpaddr19[G‑1]**, then write that 0 back, thereby updating the underlying value of **pmpaddr19[G‑1]** to 0.

- **Read‑modify‑write of pmpaddr19 with CSRRS or CSRRC when the G‑1 bit reads differently from its underlying value**  
  *Condition:* An executing **CSRRS** or **CSRRC** instruction accesses **pmpaddr19**, and the underlying value of **pmpaddr19[G‑1]** is 1 while a read of that bit returns 0.  
  *Effect:* The read returns 0; if the instruction modifies any other bit of **pmpaddr19**, the 0 read from **pmpaddr19[G‑1]** is written back, causing the underlying value of **pmpaddr19[G‑1]** to become 0.

- **CSRRW instruction targeting pmpaddr19**  
  *If rd = x0* – the instruction shall **not read** **pmpaddr19** and shall **write** the value in rs1 to **pmpaddr19**.  
  *If rd ≠ x0* – the instruction shall **read** the old value of **pmpaddr19**, zero‑extend it to XLEN bits, write it to rd, and **write** the value in rs1 to **pmpaddr19**.

- **CSRRS / CSRRC instruction targeting pmpaddr19**  
  *If rs1 = x0* – the instruction shall **read** **pmpaddr19**, shall **not write** to it, and shall **not cause any side effects** that might otherwise occur on a CSR write.  
  *If rs1 ≠ x0* – the instruction shall **read** **pmpaddr19**, shall **write** to it, and shall **action side effects only for fields** for which rs1 has at least one bit set corresponding to that field.

- **CSRRWI instruction targeting pmpaddr19**  
  *If rd = x0* – the instruction shall **not read** **pmpaddr19** and shall **write zero** to **pmpaddr19**.  
  *If rd ≠ x0* – the instruction shall **read** **pmpaddr19**, write the zero‑extended immediate to **pmpaddr19**, and action side effects for all fields of the written CSR.

- **CSRRSI / CSRRCI instruction targeting pmpaddr19**  
  *If uimm = 0* – the instruction shall **read** **pmpaddr19**, shall **not write** to it, and shall **not cause any side effects** that might otherwise occur on a CSR write.  
  *If uimm ≠ 0* – the instruction shall **read** **pmpaddr19**, shall **write** to it, and shall **action side effects only for fields** for which the immediate has at least one bit set corresponding to that field.

- **Side‑effect handling for pmpaddr19**  
  *CSRRW[I]* instructions **action side effects for all fields** within **pmpaddr19** when they write it.  
  *CSRRS[I] and CSRRC[I]* instructions **action side effects only for fields** of **pmpaddr19** where the rs1 register or immediate argument has at least one bit set corresponding to that field.

The following description:

- **NAPOT range encoding (Table 24)**  

  ```
  | pmpaddr   | pmpcfg .A | Match type and size        |
  |-----------|-----------|----------------------------|
  | yyyy…yyyy | NA4       | 4-byte NAPOT range         |
  | yyyy…yyy0 | NAPOT     | 8-byte NAPOT range         |
  | yyyy…yy01 | NAPOT     | 16-byte NAPOT range        |
  | yyyy…y011 | NAPOT     | 32-byte NAPOT range        |
  | …         | …         | …                          |
  | yy01…1111 | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range    |
  | y011…1111 | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range  |
  | 0111…1111 | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range  |
  | 1111…1111 | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range  |
  ```

  *When the configuration register for PMP entry 23 (`pmpcfg23.A`) selects NA4, `pmpaddr23` encodes a 4‑byte NAPOT range. When `pmpcfg23.A` selects NAPOT, the low‑order bits of `pmpaddr23` encode the size of the range according to the patterns shown in the table.*

- **Top‑of‑range (TOR) mode**  

  *If TOR is selected, the associated address register forms the top of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range.*  
  *Thus, when `pmpcfg23.A` is TOR, `pmpaddr23` is the top of the range and `pmpaddr22` is the bottom.*

- **Address matching for TOR entries**  

  *If PMP entry i's A field is set to TOR, the entry matches any address y such that `pmpaddri‑1 ≤ y < pmpaddri` (irrespective of the value of `pmpcfgi‑1`).*  
  *Consequently, for i = 23, the entry matches any address y such that `pmpaddr22 ≤ y < pmpaddr23`.*

- **No‑match condition for TOR entries**  

  *If `pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri` and `pmpcfgi.A = TOR`, then PMP entry i matches no addresses.*  
  *Therefore, if `pmpaddr22 ≥ pmpaddr23` and `pmpcfg23.A = TOR`, entry 23 matches no addresses.*

- **Granularity effect on reads of `pmpaddr23`**  

  *When G ≥ 2 and `pmpcfg23.A[1]` is set, i.e. the mode is NAPOT, then bits `pmpaddr23[G‑2:0]` read as all ones.*  

  *When G ≥ 1 and `pmpcfg23.A[1]` is clear, i.e. the mode is OFF or TOR, then bits `pmpaddr23[G‑1:0]` read as all zeros.*  

  *Bits `pmpaddr23[G‑1:0]` do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.*

- **Retention of underlying stored value**  

  *Although changing `pmpcfg23.A[1]` affects the value read from `pmpaddr23`, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register—in particular, `pmpaddr23[G‑1]` retains its original value when `pmpcfg23.A` is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT.*
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: When pmpcfg23.A selects NA4, pmpaddr23 encodes a 4‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 2: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low‑order bit of pmpaddr23 is 0, pmpaddr23 encodes an 8‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 3: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr23 are 01, pmpaddr23 encodes a 16‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 4: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr23 are 011, pmpaddr23 encodes a 32‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 5: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr23 match the pattern yy01 followed by all ones, pmpaddr23 encodes a 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 6: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr23 match the pattern y011 followed by all ones, pmpaddr23 encodes a 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 7: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr23 match the pattern 0111 followed by all ones, pmpaddr23 encodes a 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 8: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr23 are all ones, pmpaddr23 encodes a 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 9: When pmpcfg23.A selects TOR, pmpaddr23 provides the top address of the range while pmpaddr22 provides the bottom address of the range.  
RULE 10: When pmpcfg23.A selects TOR, entry 23 matches any address y such that pmpaddr22 ≤ y < pmpaddr23.  
RULE 11: If pmpaddr22 ≥ pmpaddr23 and pmpcfg23.A selects TOR, then entry 23 matches no addresses.  
RULE 12: When the granularity G is at least 2 and pmpcfg23.A[1] is set (indicating NAPOT mode), bits pmpaddr23[G‑2:0] read as all ones.  
RULE 13: When the granularity G is at least 1 and pmpcfg23.A[1] is clear (indicating OFF or TOR mode), bits pmpaddr23[G‑1:0] read as all zeros.  
RULE 14: Bits pmpaddr23[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.

- If TOR is selected, the associated address register forms the top of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range. Hence, when pmpcfg25.A = TOR, pmpaddr25 is the top of the range and pmpaddr24 is the bottom of the range.

- If pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri and pmpcfgi.A = TOR, then PMP entry i matches no addresses. Applied to i = 25, if pmpaddr24 ≥ pmpaddr25 and pmpcfg25.A = TOR, then entry 25 matches no addresses.

- When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg i.A[1] is set, i.e., the mode is NAPOT, then bits pmpaddr i[G‑2:0] read as all ones. Thus, for i = 25, if G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg25.A[1] = 1, bits pmpaddr25[G‑2:0] read as all ones.

- When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg i.A[1] is clear, i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR, then bits pmpaddr i[G‑1:0] read as all zeros. Thus, for i = 25, if G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg25.A[1] = 0, bits pmpaddr25[G‑1:0] read as all zeros.

- Bits pmpaddr i[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic. Therefore, bits pmpaddr25[G‑1:0] are ignored by the TOR matching mechanism for entry 25.

- Although changing pmpcfg i.A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddr i, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register—in particular, pmpaddr i[G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg i.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT. Consequently, for i = 25, pmpaddr25[G‑1] retains its original stored value when pmpcfg25.A is changed between NAPOT and TOR/OFF.
============================================================

RULE 1: The interpretation of pmpaddr25 is determined by the A field of pmpcfg25.  
RULE 2: When pmpcfg25.A selects NAPOT, the low‑order bits of pmpaddr25 encode the size of the NAPOT region.  
RULE 3: When pmpcfg25.A = TOR, pmpaddr25 serves as the top address of the range.

The following description:

- **CSRRS and CSRRC behavior affecting pmpaddr27**

The following description:

- **A field encoding (Table 23)** – "The A field in a PMP entry's configuration register encodes the address‑matching mode of the associated PMP address register."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr27*: the value of **pmpcfg27.A** determines how **pmpaddr27** is interpreted (OFF, TOR, NA4, or NAPOT).

- **NAPOT range encoding (Table 24)** – The low‑order bits of the associated address register encode the size of a NAPOT range as shown:

| pmpaddr pattern | pmpcfg .A | Match type and size |
|-----------------|-----------|----------------------|
| yyyy…yyyy       | NA4       | 4‑byte NAPOT range |
| yyyy…yyy0       | NAPOT     | 8‑byte NAPOT range |
| yyyy…yy01       | NAPOT     | 16‑byte NAPOT range |
| yyyy…y011       | NAPOT     | 32‑byte NAPOT range |
| …               | …         | … |
| yy01…1111       | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range |
| y011…1111       | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range |
| 0111…1111       | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
| 1111…1111       | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

*Effect on pmpaddr27*: when **pmpcfg27.A = NAPOT**, the pattern of the low bits of **pmpaddr27** determines the size of the matched region exactly as listed.

- **TOR mode address‑matching** – "If TOR is selected, the associated address register forms the top of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr27*: when **pmpcfg27.A = TOR**, **pmpaddr27** is the *top* of the range; **pmpaddr26** is the *bottom*.

- **TOR match condition** – "If PMP entry i's A field is set to TOR, the entry matches any address y such that pmpaddri‑1 ≤ y < pmpaddri (irrespective of the value of pmpcfgi‑1)."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr27*: when **pmpcfg27.A = TOR**, the entry matches any address y such that **pmpaddr26 ≤ y < pmpaddr27**, regardless of **pmpcfg26**.

- **TOR empty‑range condition** – "If pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri and pmpcfgi.A = TOR, then PMP entry i matches no addresses."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr27*: if **pmpaddr26 ≥ pmpaddr27** while **pmpcfg27.A = TOR**, entry 27 matches no addresses.

- **Granularity‑related read masking** –  
  1. "When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg i.A[1] is set, i.e. the mode is NAPOT, then bits pmpaddri[G‑2:0] read as all ones."  
     *Effect on pmpaddr27*: if the implementation's granularity G ≥ 2 and **pmpcfg27.A[1] = 1** (NAPOT), reads of **pmpaddr27** return ones in bits **[G‑2:0]**.  
  2. "When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfgi.A[1] is clear, i.e. the mode is OFF or TOR, then bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] read as all zeros."  
     *Effect on pmpaddr27*: if G ≥ 1 and **pmpcfg27.A[1] = 0** (OFF or TOR), reads of **pmpaddr27** return zeros in bits **[G‑1:0]**.  
  3. "Bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic."  
     *Effect on pmpaddr27*: the masked‑out low bits of **pmpaddr27** are ignored when **pmpcfg27.A = TOR**.  
  4. "Although changing pmpcfgi.A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddri, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register—in particular, pmpaddr i [G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg i.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT."  
     *Effect on pmpaddr27*: the physical bit **pmpaddr27[G‑1]** is preserved when **pmpcfg27.A** is switched between NAPOT and TOR/OFF and later returned to NAPOT.

RULE 3: When pmpcfg27.A = TOR, pmpaddr27 provides the top address of the range while pmpaddr26 provides the bottom address.

RULE 7: When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg27.A[1] = 0 (OFF or TOR mode), reads of pmpaddr27 return all zeros in bits G‑1 down to 0.  
RULE 8: The low bits of pmpaddr27 masked by granularity (bits G‑1 down to 0) are ignored by the TOR address‑matching logic.  
RULE 9: The physical bit pmpaddr27[G‑1] retains its original stored value when pmpcfg27.A is changed between NAPOT and OFF/TOR modes, even though the read value of pmpaddr27 may change.

The following description:

- **CSR instruction atomicity** – Any CSR instruction that specifies the CSR address for pmpaddr28 (the CSR specifier is encoded in bits 31‑20 of the instruction) "atomically read‑modify‑write a single CSR"【source】.  

- **CSRRW on pmpaddr28** – The CSRRW instruction "reads the old value of the CSR, zero‑extends the value to XLEN bits, then writes it to integer register rd. The initial value in rs1 is written to the CSR." If rd = x0, "the instruction shall not read the CSR and shall not cause any of the side effects that might occur on a CSR read." A CSRRW with rs1 = x0 "will attempt to write zero to the destination CSR"【source】.  

- **CSRRS on pmpaddr28** – The CSRRS instruction "reads the value of the CSR, zero‑extends the value to XLEN bits, and writes it to integer register rd. The initial value in integer register rs1 is treated as a bit mask that specifies bit positions to be set in the CSR. Any bit that is high in rs1 will cause the corresponding bit to be set in the CSR, if that CSR bit is writable."  

- **CSRRC on pmpaddr28** – The CSRRC instruction "reads the value of the CSR, zero‑extends the value to XLEN bits, and writes it to integer register rd. The initial value in integer register rs1 is treated as a bit mask that specifies bit positions to be cleared in the CSR. Any bit that is high in rs1 will cause the corresponding bit to be cleared in the CSR, if that CSR bit is writable."  

- **Read‑modify‑write side effect when underlying bits differ** – "Since CSRRS and CSRRC perform a read‑modify‑write operation, any bits that read as a different value to their underlying value may be modified by these instructions even if the corresponding bit is not set in rs1. For example, **pmpaddrn[G‑1] may have an underlying value of 1 but read as 0**. Executing CSRRC or CSRRS to modify a different bit will cause 0 to be read from **pmpaddrn[G‑1]** and then written back, updating the underlying value to 0." Therefore, when n = 28 the same behavior applies to **pmpaddr28[G‑1]**.  

- **CSRRS/CSRRC write‑disable condition** – "For both CSRRS and CSRRC, if rs1 = x0, then the instruction will not write to the CSR at all, and so shall not cause any of the side effects that might otherwise occur on a CSR write, nor raise illegal‑instruction exceptions on accesses to read‑only CSRs. Both CSRRS and CSRRC always read the addressed CSR and cause any read side effects regardless of rs1 and rd fields."  

- **Zero‑value rs1 does not trigger per‑field side effects** – "Note that if rs1 specifies a register other than x0, and that register holds a zero value, the instruction will not action any attendant per‑field side effects, but will action any side effects caused by writing to the entire CSR."  

- **Immediate‑form instructions on pmpaddr28** – The CSRRWI, CSRRSI, and CSRRCI variants behave as described for their register‑operand counterparts, except they use a zero‑extended 5‑bit immediate. For CSRRSI and CSRRCI, "if the uimm[4:0] field is zero, then these instructions will not write to the CSR, and shall not cause any of the side effects that might otherwise occur on a CSR write, nor raise illegal‑instruction exceptions on accesses to read‑only CSRs."  

- **Table 7 (conditions for reading/writing a CSR)** – The rows that apply to pmpaddr28 are:

| Instruction | rd is x0? | rs1 is x0? / uimm=0? | Reads CSR? | Writes CSR? |
|-------------|-----------|----------------------|------------|-------------|
| CSRRW       | Yes       | –                    | No         | Yes |
| CSRRW       | No        | –                    | Yes        | Yes |
| CSRRS/CSRRC| –         | Yes                  | Yes        | No |
| CSRRS/CSRRC| –         | No                   | Yes        | Yes |
| CSRRWI      | Yes       | –                    | No         | Yes |
| CSRRWI      | No        | –                    | Yes        | Yes |
| CSRRSI/CSRRCI| –       | Yes                  | Yes        | No |
| CSRRSI/CSRRCI| –       | No                   | Yes        | Yes |

(Exact wording taken from the source table.)  

- **Side‑effects on field writes** – "As of this writing, **no standard CSRs have side effects on field writes**." Since pmpaddr28 is a standard CSR, it inherits this property.  

- **Side‑effects on writes (indirect effects only)** – "Standard CSRs may have side effects on writes. … Indirect effects of a CSR write are not considered by the RISC‑V ISA to be side effects of that write."  

- **Special CSRs with automatic updates** – The text notes that "some CSRs, such as the instructions‑retired counter, instret, may be modified as side effects of instruction execution." pmpaddr28 is **not** listed among these, so no automatic update side effect applies.

The following description:

- **Address‑matching mode selection** – The A field in a PMP entry's configuration register determines how the associated PMP address register (including pmpaddr28) is used for address matching.  
  - When A = 0 the entry is disabled and matches no addresses.  
  - When A = 1 the entry uses TOR (top‑of‑range) mode.  
  - When A = 2 the entry uses NA4 (naturally aligned four‑byte) mode.  
  - When A = 3 the entry uses NAPOT (naturally aligned power‑of‑two) mode.

- **TOR mode behavior** – If TOR is selected, the associated address register forms the top of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range.  
  - If PMP entry *i*'s A field is set to TOR, the entry matches any address *y* such that **pmpaddri‑1 ≤ y < pmpaddri** (irrespective of the value of pmpcfgi‑1).  
  - If PMP entry 0's A field is set to TOR, zero is used for the lower bound, and so it matches any address *y < pmpaddr0*.  
  - If **pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri** and **pmpcfgi.A = TOR**, then PMP entry *i* matches no addresses.

- **NAPOT range encoding (Table 24)** – When the A field of the configuration register for the entry that uses pmpaddr28 is set to NA4 or NAPOT, the low‑order bits of pmpaddr28 encode the size of the range as follows:

  | pmpaddr bits pattern | pmpcfg.A | Match type and size |
  |----------------------|----------|---------------------|
  | yyyy…yyyy            | NA4      | 4‑byte NAPOT range  |
  | yyyy…yyy0            | NAPOT    | 8‑byte NAPOT range  |
  | yyyy…yy01            | NAPOT    | 16‑byte NAPOT range |
  | yyyy…y011            | NAPOT    | 32‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …                    | …        | … |
  | yy01…1111            | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range |
  | y011…1111            | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range |
  | 0111…1111            | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
  | 1111…1111            | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

- **Granularity constraints affecting pmpaddr28** – The PMP granularity G influences the bits of pmpaddr28 that are read:

  - When **G ≥ 1**, the NA4 mode is not selectable.  
  - When **G ≥ 2** and **pmpcfg i.A[1]** is set (i.e., the mode is NAPOT), then **bits pmpaddri[G‑2:0] read as all ones**.  
  - When **G ≥ 1** and **pmpcfg i.A[1]** is clear (i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR), then **bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] read as all zeros**.  
  - **Bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic**.  
  - **Although changing pmpcfg i.A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddri, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register—in particular, pmpaddr i[G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg i.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT**.

- **TOR address‑matching using pmpaddr30**

The following description:

- The A field in a PMP entry's configuration register **encodes the address‑matching mode of the associated PMP address register**; therefore the A field of **pmpcfg34** determines the matching mode of **pmpaddr34**.  

- When **pmpcfg34.A = 0** (OFF), **pmpaddr34** is **disabled and matches no addresses**.  

- When **pmpcfg34.A = 1** (TOR), **pmpaddr34** **forms the top of the address range** and the preceding PMP address register (**pmpaddr33**) **forms the bottom of the address range**.  In this case the entry matches any address *y* such that **pmpaddr33 ≤ y < pmpaddr34** (irrespective of the value of **pmpcfg33**).  

- If **pmpaddr33 ≥ pmpaddr34** and **pmpcfg34.A = TOR**, then **pmpaddr34** **matches no addresses**.  

- When **pmpcfg34.A = 2** (NA4), the low‑order bits of **pmpaddr34** encode a **4‑byte NAPOT range** (pattern "yyyy…yyyy").  

- When **pmpcfg34.A = 3** (NAPOT), the low‑order bits of **pmpaddr34** encode the size of the NAPOT range according to Table 24, e.g.:  
  - pattern "yyyy…yyy0" -> 8‑byte NAPOT range,  
  - pattern "yyyy…yy01" -> 16‑byte NAPOT range,  
  - pattern "yyyy…y011" -> 32‑byte NAPOT range, …, up to the patterns that encode the maximum 2 XLEN‑byte range.  

- **It is not possible to represent the address 2 XLEN+2 as the top of a range**, so in an **RV32 system with 34‑bit physical addresses**, a TOR PMP **cannot be used** to give less‑privileged modes access to the uppermost word of memory; a **NAPOT PMP can be used**, or that memory can be left inaccessible. (Thus **pmpaddr34** cannot serve as the top of a TOR range for the uppermost word in such a system.)  

- The PMP granularity is **2^(G+2) bytes** and **must be the same across all PMP regions**.  

- When **G ≥ 2** and **pmpcfg34.A[1] is set** (mode NAPOT), **bits pmpaddr34[G‑2:0] read as all ones**.  

- When **G ≥ 1** and **pmpcfg34.A[1] is clear** (mode OFF or TOR), **bits pmpaddr34[G‑1:0] read as all zeros**.  

- **Bits pmpaddr34[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic**.

  |-------------------|---------------------|

  | `yyyy…yy01`       | 16‑byte NAPOT range |

  | `yy01…1111`       | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range |
  | `y011…1111`       | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range |
  | `0111…1111`       | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
  | `1111…1111`       | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

The following description:

- **pmpaddr37 is a PMP address CSR.** The text states that a PMP address register (pmpaddr n) "may have an underlying value of 1 but read as 0." This applies to any pmpaddr register, including pmpaddr37.

- **Read‑modify‑write of pmpaddr37 with CSRRS/CSRRC can change hidden bits.**  
  *If an instruction such as CSRRS or CSRRC modifies a bit other than the top‑most PMP address bit (pmpaddr n[G‑1]), the hardware will read the current *read* value of pmpaddr n[G‑1] (which may be 0 even if the underlying value is 1), write that read value back, and thereby update the underlying value to match the read value (i.e., set it to 0).*

- **CSRRS and CSRRC always read pmpaddr37.**  
  *"Both CSRRS and CSRRC always read the addressed CSR and cause any read side effects regardless of rs1 and rd fields."*  
  Therefore, any execution of CSRRS/CSRRC that targets pmpaddr37 reads its current value and triggers any read side effects defined for that CSR.

- **Writing behavior of CSRRS/CSRRC on pmpaddr37.**  
  *If rs1 = x0, then the instruction will not write to the CSR at all, and so shall not cause any of the side effects that might otherwise occur on a CSR write.*  
  *If rs1 ≠ x0, the instruction will write to the CSR (including pmpaddr37). The write will "action side effects for fields for which the rs1 … argument has at least one bit set corresponding to that field."*  
  *If rs1 specifies a register other than x0 and that register holds zero, the instruction will not action any attendant per‑field side effects, but will action any side effects caused by writing to the entire CSR.*

- **Table 7 conditions for CSRRS/CSRRC on pmpaddr37.**  
  | rs1 field | Reads pmpaddr37? | Writes pmpaddr37? |
  |-----------|------------------|-------------------|
  | x0        | Yes              | No                |
  | not x0    | Yes              | Yes               |

- **Immediate‑operand variants on pmpaddr37 (CSRRSI/CSRRCI).**  
  *For CSRRSI and CSRRCI, if the uimm[4:0] field is zero, then these instructions will not write to the CSR, and shall not cause any of the side effects that might otherwise occur on a CSR write.*  
  *Otherwise (uimm ≠ 0), the instruction reads and writes the CSR (including pmpaddr37) and follows the same per‑field side‑effect rules as CSRRS/CSRRC.*  

- **CSRRW behavior on pmpaddr37.**  
  *A CSRRW with rs1 = x0 will attempt to write zero to the destination CSR.*  
  Thus, executing CSRRW targeting pmpaddr37 with rs1 = x0 will write the value 0 into pmpaddr37.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: pmpaddr37 is a PMP address CSR.  
RULE 2: pmpaddr37 may have an underlying value of 1 but read as 0.  
RULE 3: If a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction modifies a bit other than the top‑most PMP address bit of pmpaddr37, the hardware must read the current read value of pmpaddr37[G‑1] (which may be 0 even if the underlying value is 1), must write that read value back, and must update the underlying value of that bit to match the read value.  
RULE 4: CSRRS and CSRRC always read pmpaddr37 and cause any read side effects defined for pmpaddr37 regardless of the rs1 and rd fields.  
RULE 5: CSRRS or CSRRC with rs1 = x0 must not write to pmpaddr37 and shall not cause any write side effects on pmpaddr37.  
RULE 6: CSRRS or CSRRC with rs1 ≠ x0 must write to pmpaddr37 and must trigger side effects for any fields whose corresponding bits are set in rs1.  
RULE 7: CSRRS or CSRRC with rs1 ≠ x0 and with the source register containing zero must not trigger per‑field side effects on pmpaddr37 but must trigger any side effects associated with writing the entire CSR.  
RULE 8: For any CSRRS or CSRRC targeting pmpaddr37, the CSR is always read and it is written only when rs1 ≠ x0.  
RULE 9: CSRRSI or CSRRCI with uimm[4:0] = 0 shall not write to pmpaddr37 and shall not cause any write side effects on pmpaddr37.  
RULE 10: CSRRSI or CSRRCI with uimm[4:0] ≠ 0 must read and write pmpaddr37 and must follow the same per‑field side‑effect rules as CSRRS or CSRRC.  
RULE 11: A CSRRW targeting pmpaddr37 with rs1 = x0 must write the value 0 into pmpaddr37.

- The A field in a PMP entry's configuration register encodes the address‑matching mode of the associated PMP address register; therefore the A field in **pmpcfg37** determines the matching mode used for **pmpaddr37**.

- Table 24 (excerpt) – encoding of the low‑order bits of a PMP address register (applies to **pmpaddr37**):
  - `yyyy…yyyy` with **pmpcfg.A = 2** (NA4) -> 4‑byte NAPOT range

  - `yyyy…yy01` with **pmpcfg.A = 3** (NAPOT) -> 16‑byte NAPOT range  
  - `yyyy…y011` with **pmpcfg.A = 3** (NAPOT) -> 32‑byte NAPOT range  
  - … (continues up to the pattern `1111…1111` for a 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range)

- If TOR is selected, the associated address register forms the top of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range; thus for entry 37, **pmpaddr37** is the top bound of the range and the entry matches any address y such that `pmpaddr36 ≤ y < pmpaddr37` (irrespective of the value of **pmpcfg36**).

- If **pmpcfg0.A = TOR**, zero is used for the lower bound, and the entry matches any address y < `pmpaddr0`. (This rule does not involve **pmpaddr37**.)

- If `pmpaddr(i‑1) ≥ pmpaddr(i)` and **pmpcfg(i).A = TOR**, then PMP entry i matches no addresses; therefore, if `pmpaddr36 ≥ pmpaddr37` and **pmpcfg37.A = TOR**, entry 37 matches no addresses.

- "In general, the PMP grain is 2 G+2 bytes and **must** be the same across all PMP regions." (Applies to the granularity that affects how **pmpaddr37** is interpreted.)

- When G ≥ 1, the NA4 mode is not selectable. (Relevant if the implementation defines G ≥ 1; it prevents **pmpcfg37.A = 2**.)

- When G ≥ 2 and **pmpcfg37.A[1]** is set (i.e., the mode is NAPOT), then bits `pmpaddr37[G‑2:0]` **read as all ones**.

- When G ≥ 1 and **pmpcfg37.A[1]** is clear (i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR), then bits `pmpaddr37[G‑1:0]` **read as all zeros**.

- Bits `pmpaddr37[G‑1:0]` **do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic**.

RULE 2: When pmpcfg37.A = 3, the low‑order bits of pmpaddr37 encode the size of the NAPOT region.  
RULE 3: With pmpcfg37.A = 2 (NA4), the low‑order bits of pmpaddr37 are all ones and represent a 4‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 4: With pmpcfg37.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr37 ending in 0, the encoded region size is 8 bytes.  
RULE 5: With pmpcfg37.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr37 ending in 01, the encoded region size is 16 bytes.

The following description:

- **pmpaddr38 is a PMP address CSR.**  
  The PMP address registers are CSRs named pmpaddr0 ‑ pmpaddr63; therefore pmpaddr38 is one of these CSRs.  

- **Encoding of address bits (RV32).**  
  For RV32, each PMP address register, including pmpaddr38, encodes bits 33‑2 of a 34‑bit physical address.  

- **Encoding of address bits (RV64).**  
  For RV64, each PMP address register, including pmpaddr38, encodes bits 55‑2 of a 56‑bit physical address.  

- **WARL property.**  
  Not all physical address bits may be implemented, and so the pmpaddr registers are WARL; consequently pmpaddr38 is a WARL register and may be read‑only zero.  

- **M‑mode accessibility.**  
  PMP CSRs are only accessible to M‑mode; therefore pmpaddr38 can be accessed only while the hart is in M‑mode.  

- **Entry implementation ordering.**  
  Up to 64 PMP entries are supported. Implementations may implement zero, 16, or 64 PMP entries; the lowest‑numbered PMP entries must be implemented first. Hence, if an implementation supports fewer than 39 entries, pmpaddr38 (which corresponds to entry 38) is not required to be implemented and, if unimplemented, behaves as a WARL register that may read as zero.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: pmpaddr38 is a PMP address control and status register (CSR) among the set pmpaddr0‑pmpaddr63.  
RULE 2: In RV32, pmpaddr38 encodes bits 33‑2 of a 34‑bit physical address.  
RULE 3: In RV64, pmpaddr38 encodes bits 55‑2 of a 56‑bit physical address.  
RULE 4: pmpaddr38 is a WARL (write‑any‑value‑read‑legal) register and may read as zero.  
RULE 5: pmpaddr38 is accessible only while the hart is executing in M‑mode.  
RULE 6: Implementations must implement PMP entries in order of increasing entry number, therefore pmpaddr38 can be implemented only if entries 0 through 37 are also implemented.  
RULE 7: If an implementation supports fewer than 39 PMP entries, pmpaddr38 is not required to be implemented.  
RULE 8: When pmpaddr38 is not implemented, it behaves as a WARL register that may read as zero.

  | …0111…1111                     | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT |
  | …1111…1111                     | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT |

  *When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg39.A[1] is clear (i.e., mode is OFF or TOR), bits pmpaddr39[G‑1:0] read as all zeros. These bits do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.*

- **TOR address‑matching** – "If TOR is selected, the associated address register forms the top of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr41*: when **pmpcfg41.A = TOR**, **pmpaddr41** is the top of the range and **pmpaddr40** (the preceding address register) is the bottom.

- **TOR matching rule** – "If PMP entry *i*'s A field is set to TOR, the entry matches any address *y* such that *pmpaddri‑1* ≤ *y* < *pmpaddri* (irrespective of the value of *pmpcfgi‑1*)."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr41*: when **pmpcfg41.A = TOR**, the entry matches any address *y* such that **pmpaddr40** ≤ *y* < **pmpaddr41**, regardless of **pmpcfg40**.

- **TOR lower‑bound for entry 0** – "If PMP entry 0's A field is set to TOR, zero is used for the lower bound, and so it matches any address *y* < *pmpaddr0*."  
  *Not directly applicable to pmpaddr41* (only entry 0).

- **TOR with inverted bounds** – "If *pmpaddri‑1* ≥ *pmpaddri* and *pmpcfgi.A = TOR*, then PMP entry *i* matches no addresses."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr41*: if **pmpaddr40** ≥ **pmpaddr41** while **pmpcfg41.A = TOR**, the entry matches no addresses.

- **Granularity constraints** – "In general, the PMP grain is 2^G+2 bytes and must be the same across all PMP regions."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr41*: the granularity that applies to **pmpaddr41** must be the same as for every other PMP region.

- **Effect of granularity *G* on read values (NAPOT)** – "When *G* ≥ 2 and *pmpcfg i.A[1]* is set, i.e. the mode is NAPOT, then bits *pmpaddri[G‑2:0]* read as all ones."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr41*: if the system's granularity *G* ≥ 2 and **pmpcfg41.A = NAPOT**, reading **pmpaddr41** yields ones in bits *[G‑2:0]*.

- **Effect of granularity *G* on read values (OFF/TOR)** – "When *G* ≥ 1 and *pmpcfgi.A[1]* is clear, i.e. the mode is OFF or TOR, then bits *pmpaddri[G‑1:0]* read as all zeros."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr41*: if *G* ≥ 1 and **pmpcfg41.A** is OFF or TOR, reading **pmpaddr41** yields zeros in bits *[G‑1:0]*.

- **Read‑value vs. stored value** – "Although changing *pmpcfgi.A[1]* affects the value read from *pmpaddri*, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register—in particular, *pmpaddr i[G‑1]* retains its original value when *pmpcfg i.A* is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT."

  *Effect on pmpaddr41*: if the system granularity *G* ≥ 1, **pmpaddr41** cannot be used with the NA4 matching mode.

  | 0111…1111 | NAPOT | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
  | 1111…1111 | NAPOT | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

- **If TOR is selected, the associated address register forms the top of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range.**  
  *(Thus, when pmpcfg42.A = TOR, pmpaddr42 is the top of the range and pmpaddr41 is the bottom.)*

  *(For i = 42 this applies when pmpaddr41 ≥ pmpaddr42 and pmpcfg42.A = TOR.)*

- **When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg i .A[1] is set, i.e. the mode is NAPOT, then bits pmpaddri[G‑2:0] read as all ones.**  
  *(Applies to pmpaddr42 under the same conditions.)*

- **When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfgi.A[1] is clear, i.e. the mode is OFF or TOR, then bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] read as all zeros.**  
  *(Applies to pmpaddr42 under the same conditions.)*

- **Bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.**  
  *(Thus, for pmpaddr42 the low‑order G bits are ignored when pmpcfg42.A = TOR.)*

- **Although changing pmpcfgi.A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddri, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register—in particular, pmpaddr i [G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg i .A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT.**

- When the A field of PMP entry 44's configuration register is **NA4**, the low‑order bits of **pmpaddr44** are interpreted as "yyyy…yyyy" and the entry matches a 4‑byte NAPOT range (Table 24).

  * "yyyy…yyy0" -> 8‑byte NAPOT range  
  * "yyyy…yy01" -> 16‑byte NAPOT range  
  * "yyyy…y011" -> 32‑byte NAPOT range  
  * … (continuing pattern) …  
  * "yy01…1111" -> 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range  
  * "y011…1111" -> 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range  
  * "0111…1111" -> 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range  
  * "1111…1111" -> 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range

The entry matches any address y such that **pmpaddr43 ≤ y < pmpaddr44**, irrespective of the value of **pmpcfg43.A**.

- If **pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri** and **pmpcfgi.A = TOR**, then PMP entry i matches no addresses. (Thus, if **pmpaddr43 ≥ pmpaddr44** and **pmpcfg44.A = TOR**, entry 44 matches no addresses.)

- When **G ≥ 1** and **pmpcfg44.A[1]** is clear (i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR), then bits **pmpaddr44[G‑1:0]** read as all zeros.

- Bits **pmpaddr44[G‑1:0]** do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.

- Changing **pmpcfg44.A[1]** affects the value read from **pmpaddr44**, but does **not** affect the underlying value stored in that register; in particular, **pmpaddr44[G‑1]** retains its original value when **pmpcfg44.A** is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT.

The following description:

- **A field encoding (Table 23)**  
  The A field in the PMP entry's configuration register (pmpcfg45.A) determines the address‑matching mode of the associated address register (pmpaddr45).  
  * A = 0 -> OFF (null region, disabled, matches no addresses)  
  * A = 1 -> TOR (top of range)  
  * A = 2 -> NA4 (naturally aligned four‑byte region)  
  * A = 3 -> NAPOT (naturally aligned power‑of‑two region, ≥ 8 bytes)

- **NAPOT range encoding (Table 24) – effect on pmpaddr45**  
  When pmpcfg45.A = 2 (NA4) or 3 (NAPOT), the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 encode the size of the range as follows (the "y" bits denote the most‑significant bits of the register, which are unchanged by the encoding):  

  | pmpaddr45 bits (low‑order) | pmpcfg45.A | Match type and size |
  |----------------------------|------------|---------------------|
  | …yyyy…yyyy                 | NA4        | 4‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …yyyy…yyy0                | NAPOT      | 8‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …yyyy…yy01                | NAPOT      | 16‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …yyyy…y011                | NAPOT      | 32‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …                         | …          | … |
  | …yy01…1111                | NAPOT      | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …y011…1111                | NAPOT      | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …0111…1111                | NAPOT      | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …1111…1111                | NAPOT      | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

- **TOR address‑matching behavior involving pmpaddr45**  
  *If pmpcfg45.A = TOR* the associated address register (pmpaddr45) forms the **top** of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register (pmpaddr44) forms the **bottom** of the range. The entry matches any address y such that  

  `pmpaddr44 ≤ y < pmpaddr45`  

  (the value of pmpcfg44.A is irrelevant).  

  *If pmpcfg0.A = TOR* (i.e., entry 0), the lower bound is zero, so the entry matches any address y < pmpaddr0. (This rule is not specific to pmpaddr45 but shows the general TOR semantics.)

- **TOR with inverted bounds**  
  If `pmpaddr44 ≥ pmpaddr45` **and** `pmpcfg45.A = TOR`, then PMP entry 45 matches **no addresses**.

- **Granularity‑related read‑mask behavior affecting pmpaddr45**  
  Let **G** be the PMP granularity (derived from the least‑significant one‑bit of pmpaddr0 after the "determine‑granularity" procedure). Then:  

  * When `G ≥ 2` **and** `pmpcfg45.A[1]` is set (i.e., mode NAPOT), bits `pmpaddr45[G‑2:0]` read as all ones.  

  * When `G ≥ 1` **and** `pmpcfg45.A[1]` is clear (i.e., mode OFF or TOR), bits `pmpaddr45[G‑1:0]` read as all zeros.  

  * Bits `pmpaddr45[G‑1:0]` do **not** affect the TOR address‑matching logic.  

  * Changing `pmpcfg45.A[1]` (e.g., from NAPOT to TOR/OFF or back) **does not** change the underlying stored value of `pmpaddr45`; specifically, `pmpaddr45[G‑1]` retains its original value when the mode is changed and later restored to NAPOT.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: If pmpcfg45.A = 0 then pmpaddr45 operates in OFF mode, defining a null region that is disabled and matches no addresses.  
RULE 2: If pmpcfg45.A = 1 then pmpaddr45 operates in TOR mode, acting as the top of an address range whose bottom is defined by pmpaddr44.  
RULE 3: If pmpcfg45.A = 2 then pmpaddr45 operates in NA4 mode, defining a naturally aligned four‑byte region.  
RULE 4: If pmpcfg45.A = 3 then pmpaddr45 operates in NAPOT mode, defining a naturally aligned power‑of‑two region of size at least eight bytes.  
RULE 5: When pmpcfg45.A = 2 (NA4) the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 encode a 4‑byte NAPOT range, with the most‑significant bits (the "y" bits) unchanged.  
RULE 6: When pmpcfg45.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 end in 0 (pattern …yyy0) the register encodes an 8‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 7: When pmpcfg45.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 end in 01 (pattern …yy01) the register encodes a 16‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 8: When pmpcfg45.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 end in 011 (pattern …y011) the register encodes a 32‑byte NAPOT range.  
RULE 9: When pmpcfg45.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 match the pattern …yy01…1111 the register encodes a NAPOT range of size 2 × XLEN bytes.  
RULE 10: When pmpcfg45.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 match the pattern …y011…1111 the register encodes a NAPOT range of size 2 × XLEN + 1 bytes.  
RULE 11: When pmpcfg45.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 match the pattern …0111…1111 the register encodes a NAPOT range of size 2 × XLEN + 2 bytes.  
RULE 12: When pmpcfg45.A = 3 (NAPOT) and the low‑order bits of pmpaddr45 match the pattern …1111…1111 the register encodes a NAPOT range of size 2 × XLEN + 3 bytes.  
RULE 13: If pmpcfg45.A = TOR then an address y matches the PMP entry 45 precisely when pmpaddr44 ≤ y < pmpaddr45, regardless of the value of pmpcfg44.A.  
RULE 14: If pmpcfg45.A = TOR and pmpaddr44 ≥ pmpaddr45 then PMP entry 45 matches no addresses.  
RULE 15: When the granularity G is at least 2 and pmpcfg45.A[1] is set (indicating NAPOT mode), the bits pmpaddr45[G‑2:0] read as all ones.  
RULE 16: When the granularity G is at least 1 and pmpcfg45.A[1] is clear (indicating OFF or TOR mode), the bits pmpaddr45[G‑1:0] read as all zeros.  
RULE 17: Bits pmpaddr45[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic for PMP entry 45.  
RULE 18: Changing pmpcfg45.A[1] does not alter the stored value of pmpaddr45, and the bit pmpaddr45[G‑1] retains its original value when the mode is changed away from and later restored to NAPOT.

The following description:

- The A field in a PMP entry's configuration register **encodes the address‑matching mode of the associated PMP address register**. Thus the behavior of **pmpaddr46** is determined by the value of **pmpcfg46.A**.

- **If PMP entry i's A field is set to TOR**, the entry matches any address y such that **pmpaddri‑1 ≤ y < pmpaddri** (irrespective of the value of pmpcfgi‑1). For **i = 46** this means:
  * **pmpaddr46** forms the **top of the address range**,
  * **pmpaddr45** forms the **bottom of the address range**, and
  * the entry matches any address y such that **pmpaddr45 ≤ y < pmpaddr46**.

- **If pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri and pmpcfgi.A = TOR**, then **PMP entry i matches no addresses**. For **i = 46** this condition is **pmpaddr45 ≥ pmpaddr46** while **pmpcfg46.A = TOR**.

- **NAPOT ranges make use of the low‑order bits of the associated address register to encode the size of the range**, as shown in Table 24. Therefore, when **pmpcfg46.A = NAPOT**, the low‑order bits of **pmpaddr46** determine the NAPOT range size according to the patterns in Table 24.

- **When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg i .A[1] is set (i.e., the mode is NAPOT), then bits pmpaddri[G‑2:0] read as all ones.** Applied to **pmpaddr46**, if the platform granularity G ≥ 2 and **pmpcfg46.A[1] = 1**, reading **pmpaddr46** yields all‑ones in bits **[G‑2:0]**.

- **When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg i .A[1] is clear (i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR), then bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] read as all zeros.** Applied to **pmpaddr46**, if the platform granularity G ≥ 1 and **pmpcfg46.A[1] = 0**, reading **pmpaddr46** yields all‑zeros in bits **[G‑1:0]**.

- **Bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.** Thus, for **pmpaddr46** used in TOR mode, the values of bits **[G‑1:0]** are ignored when determining whether an address falls within the range.

- **Changing pmpcfg i .A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddri, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register – in particular, pmpaddr i [G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg i .A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT.** Consequently, for **pmpaddr46**, the bit **[G‑1]** preserves its stored value across changes of **pmpcfg46.A[1]** between NAPOT and TOR/OFF.

---

**Table 24. NAPOT range encoding in PMP address and configuration registers (excerpt)**  

| pmpaddr pattern | pmpcfg.A | Match type and size |
|-----------------|----------|---------------------|
| yyyy…yyyy       | NA4      | 4‑byte NAPOT range  |
| yyyy…yyy0       | NAPOT    | 8‑byte NAPOT range  |
| yyyy…yy01       | NAPOT    | 16‑byte NAPOT range |
| yyyy…y011       | NAPOT    | 32‑byte NAPOT range |
| …               | …        | …                   |
| yy01…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range |
| y011…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range |
| 0111…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
| 1111…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

The following description:

- **Register name and class**: The PMP address registers are CSRs named **pmpaddr0 – pmpaddr63**, therefore **pmpaddr50** is one of these CSRs.  

- **Accessibility**: *PMP CSRs are only accessible to M‑mode.* Consequently, **pmpaddr50** can be read or written only when the hart is in M‑mode.  

- **Supported implementations**: Implementations may implement **zero, 16, or 64** PMP entries, and *the lowest‑numbered PMP entries must be implemented first*. Therefore **pmpaddr50** is present only in implementations that support at least 51 PMP entries (i.e., the 64‑entry implementation).  

- **Encoding for RV32**: *Each PMP address register encodes bits 33‑2 of a 34‑bit physical address for RV32*, as shown in Figure 32. Thus **pmpaddr50** holds bits 33‑2 of the physical address used by PMP entry 50 when the hart implements RV32.  

- **Encoding for RV64**: *Each PMP address register encodes bits 55‑2 of a 56‑bit physical address for RV64*, as shown in Figure 33. Thus **pmpaddr50** holds bits 55‑2 of the physical address used by PMP entry 50 when the hart implements RV64.  

- **WARL property**: *Not all physical address bits may be implemented, and so the pmpaddr registers are WARL*. Therefore the value read from **pmpaddr50** may be a "write‑any‑value‑is‑read‑legal" value, and writing a value may be constrained by the implemented subset of address bits.  

- **Use of preceding entry's address register**: *Some PMP settings additionally use the address register associated with the preceding PMP entry*. Hence, when PMP entry 51 is configured to use the "top‑of‑range" (TOR) address mode, **pmpaddr50** supplies the lower bound of the address range for that entry. This behavior directly involves **pmpaddr50**.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
RULE 1: pmpaddr50 is a CSR that belongs to the set of PMP address registers named pmpaddr0 through pmpaddr63.  
RULE 2: pmpaddr50 can be read or written only when the hart is executing in M‑mode.  
RULE 3: pmpaddr50 is implemented only in implementations that provide at least 51 PMP entries, which corresponds to the 64‑entry PMP configuration.  
RULE 4: In an RV32 implementation, pmpaddr50 holds bits 33‑2 of the 34‑bit physical address used by PMP entry 50.  
RULE 5: In an RV64 implementation, pmpaddr50 holds bits 55‑2 of the 56‑bit physical address used by PMP entry 50.  
RULE 6: pmpaddr50 is a WARL register, meaning any value written may be read back, but the write may be restricted to the subset of address bits that are physically implemented.  
RULE 7: When PMP entry 51 is configured to use the top‑of‑range (TOR) address mode, pmpaddr50 supplies the lower bound of the address range for entry 51.

The following description:

- The **A field** in a PMP entry's configuration register **encodes the address‑matching mode of the associated PMP address register**.  Thus the value of pmpcfg50.A determines how pmpaddr50 is interpreted.

- **NAPOT ranges make use of the low‑order bits of the associated address register to encode the size of the range**, as shown in Table 24.  Consequently, when pmpcfg50.A = NAPOT, the low‑order bits of pmpaddr50 select the NAPOT range size.

- **Table 24 – NAPOT range encoding in PMP address and configuration registers**

  | pmpaddr pattern | pmpcfg.A | Match type and size |
  |-----------------|----------|----------------------|
  | yyyy…yyyy       | NA4      | 4‑byte NAPOT range   |
  | yyyy…yyy0       | NAPOT    | 8‑byte NAPOT range   |
  | yyyy…yy01       | NAPOT    | 16‑byte NAPOT range  |
  | yyyy…y011       | NAPOT    | 32‑byte NAPOT range  |
  | …               | …        | …                    |
  | yy01…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range |
  | y011…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range |
  | 0111…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
  | 1111…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

- **If TOR is selected, the associated address register forms the top of the address range, and the preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range.**  If PMP entry i's A field is set to TOR, **the entry matches any address y such that pmpaddri‑1 ≤ y < pmpaddri** (irrespective of the value of pmpcfgi‑1).  Therefore, when pmpcfg50.A = TOR, pmpaddr50 is the *top* of the range for entry 50, and pmpaddr49 is the *bottom*.

- **If pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri and pmpcfgi.A = TOR, then PMP entry i matches no addresses.**  Consequently, if pmpaddr49 ≥ pmpaddr50 while pmpcfg50.A = TOR, entry 50 matches no addresses.

- **When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg i.A[1] is set (i.e., the mode is NAPOT), then bits pmpaddri[G‑2:0] read as all ones.**  Thus, with a granularity G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg50.A = NAPOT, the bits pmpaddr50[G‑2:0] appear as ones when read.

- **When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg i.A[1] is clear (i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR), then bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] read as all zeros.**  Therefore, with a granularity G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg50.A = OFF or TOR, the bits pmpaddr50[G‑1:0] appear as zeros when read.

- **Bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.**  Hence, for entry 50 in TOR mode, the value of pmpaddr50[G‑1:0] is irrelevant to the matching of addresses.

- **Although changing pmpcfg i.A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddri, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register—in particular, pmpaddr i[G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg i.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT.**  Consequently, toggling pmpcfg50.A between NAPOT and TOR/OFF leaves the stored bit pmpaddr50[G‑1] unchanged.

The following description:

- **Address‑matching mode OFF (A = 0)** – If the A field of PMP entry 53 is 0, the entry is disabled and matches no addresses. The value stored in **pmpaddr53** is irrelevant for matching.  

- **Top‑of‑range (TOR) mode (A = 1)** – If the A field of PMP entry 53 is set to TOR, **pmpaddr53** forms the *top* of the address range for entry 53; the preceding address register (**pmpaddr52**) forms the *bottom* of the range. The entry matches any address *y* such that **pmpaddr52 ≤ y < pmpaddr53**, irrespective of the value of **pmpcfg52**.  

- **TOR lower‑bound zero (entry 0)** – Not applicable to **pmpaddr53** because entry 0 has no preceding register.  

- **TOR with inverted bounds** – If **pmpaddr52 ≥ pmpaddr53** and **pmpcfg53.A = TOR**, then PMP entry 53 matches no addresses.  

- **Naturally Aligned Four‑byte (NA4) mode (A = 2)** – If the A field of PMP entry 53 is NA4, the entire contents of **pmpaddr53** are used as a 4‑byte NAPOT range. The low‑order bits are not interpreted for size; the range is exactly four bytes aligned to a four‑byte boundary.  

- **Naturally Aligned Power‑of‑Two (NAPOT) mode (A = 3)** – When the A field of PMP entry 53 is NAPOT, the low‑order bits of **pmpaddr53** encode the size of the region according to Table 24:

  | Bits pattern in **pmpaddr53** (least‑significant bits) | Region size (bytes) |
  |--------------------------------------------------------|---------------------|
  | `…yyyy…yyyy` (all low bits 1)                          | 4‑byte NAPOT range  |
  | `…yyyy…yyy0`                                           | 8‑byte NAPOT range  |
  | `…yyyy…yy01`                                           | 16‑byte NAPOT range |
  | `…yyyy…y011`                                           | 32‑byte NAPOT range |
  | `…yy01…1111`                                           | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range |
  | `…y011…1111`                                           | 2 XLEN + 1‑byte NAPOT range |
  | `…0111…1111`                                           | 2 XLEN + 2‑byte NAPOT range |
  | `…1111…1111`                                           | 2 XLEN + 3‑byte NAPOT range |

  The exact pattern shown in the table applies to **pmpaddr53** when its entry's A field is NAPOT.  

- **Granularity G effect on read values** – Let *G* be the PMP granularity (2^G + 2 bytes):

  * If **G ≥ 2** and **pmpcfg53.A[1]** is set (i.e., entry 53 is in NAPOT mode), then bits **pmpaddr53[G‑2:0]** read as all ones, regardless of their stored values.  

  * If **G ≥ 1** and **pmpcfg53.A[1]** is clear (i.e., entry 53 is OFF or TOR), then bits **pmpaddr53[G‑1:0]** read as all zeros. These bits do **not** affect TOR address‑matching logic.  

- **Retention of underlying stored bits across mode changes** – Changing **pmpcfg53.A[1]** (switching between NAPOT and TOR/OFF) changes the value read from **pmpaddr53**, but does **not** change the underlying value stored in the register. The following description:

- **When the PMP entry's configuration register field A = 0 (OFF)**, the PMP entry that uses **pmpaddr55** "is disabled and matches no addresses."

  | pmpaddr pattern (low‑order bits) | A field | Match type and size |
  |----------------------------------|---------|----------------------|
  | …yyyy…yyyy                       | NA4     | 4‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …yyyy…yyy0                       | NAPOT   | 8‑byte NAPOT range |
  | …yyyy…yy01                       | NAPOT   | 16‑byte NAPOT range |

The following description:

- **Register name and set**: pmpaddr56 is one of the PMP address CSRs named pmpaddr0‑pmpaddr63.  

- **Encoding on RV64**: For RV64 harts, pmpaddr56 *encodes bits 55‑2 of a 56‑bit physical address* (Figure 33).  

- **WARL property**: All PMP address registers, including pmpaddr56, *are WARL and may be read‑only zero*.  

- **Implementation‑dependent bits**: *Not all physical address bits may be implemented, and so the pmpaddr registers are WARL*; consequently, any write to pmpaddr56 may be masked to the subset of bits that are physically implemented.  

- **Address‑matching mode dependence**: *Some PMP settings additionally use the address register associated with the preceding PMP entry*. Therefore, when PMP entry 56 is configured (e.g., in TOR address‑matching mode), pmpaddr56 may be used as the upper bound while the preceding address register (pmpaddr55) supplies the lower bound.  

- **Physical‑address limit**: The RV64 PMP address registers, including pmpaddr56, *impose the same 56‑bit physical‑address limit as the Sv48 virtual‑memory scheme*.

RESPONSE:

The following description:

- **Register name and range** – The PMP address registers are CSRs named **pmpaddr0‑pmpaddr63**; therefore **pmpaddr57** is one of these CSRs.  

- **Accessibility** – *PMP CSRs are only accessible to M‑mode.* Consequently, any read or write of **pmpaddr57** must be performed while the hart is executing in M‑mode.  

- **WARL property** – *All PMP CSR fields are WARL and may be read‑only zero.* Thus the value written to **pmpaddr57** is *write‑any‑legal‑value*; on read, the hardware may return the written value or zero.  

- **Physical‑address encoding (RV64)** – *For RV64, each PMP address register encodes bits 55‑2 of a 56‑bit physical address.* Therefore **pmpaddr57** holds bits 55‑2 of the physical address that define PMP entry 57.  

- **Physical‑address encoding (RV32)** – *Each PMP address register encodes bits 33‑2 of a 34‑bit physical address for RV32.* Accordingly, when the hart implements RV32, **pmpaddr57** holds bits 33‑2 of the physical address for PMP entry 57.  

- **Implementation‑defined bits** – *Not all physical address bits may be implemented, and so the pmpaddr registers are WARL.* Hence any bits of **pmpaddr57** that correspond to unimplemented physical‑address bits are WARL.  

- **Use of preceding address register** – *Some PMP settings additionally use the address register associated with the preceding PMP entry.* When such a setting is in effect for PMP entry 58, the hardware uses **pmpaddr57** (the preceding entry's address register) as part of the address definition for entry 58.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================

The following description:

- The **A field** in a PMP entry's configuration register encodes the address‑matching mode of the associated PMP address register.  
  *When A=0* the PMP entry is disabled and matches no addresses.  
  *When A=1 (TOR)* the associated address register forms the **top of the range**.  
  *When A=2 (NA4)* the associated address register encodes a **naturally aligned four‑byte region**.  
  *When A=3 (NAPOT)* the associated address register encodes a **naturally aligned power‑of‑two region, ≥8 bytes**.  
  This applies to **pmpaddr57** when it is the address register associated with PMP entry 57.

- **NAPOT range encoding** uses the low‑order bits of the associated address register, as shown in Table 24.  
  ```
  Table 24. NAPOT range encoding in PMP address and configuration registers.

  | pmpaddr   | pmpcfg .A | Match type and size                |
  |-----------|-----------|------------------------------------|
  | yyyy…yyyy | NA4       | 4‑byte NAPOT range                 |
  | yyyy…yyy0 | NAPOT     | 8‑byte NAPOT range                 |
  | yyyy…yy01 | NAPOT     | 16‑byte NAPOT range                |
  | yyyy…y011 | NAPOT     | 32‑byte NAPOT range                |
  | …         | …         | …                                  |
  | yy01…1111 | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range            |
  | y011…1111 | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range          |
  | 0111…1111 | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range          |
  | 1111…1111 | NAPOT     | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range          |
  ```  
  When **pmpcfg57.A = NAPOT**, the low‑order bits of **pmpaddr57** are interpreted according to this table to determine the size of the matched region.

- If **TOR** is selected, the associated address register forms the **top of the address range**, and the **preceding PMP address register forms the bottom of the address range**.  
  *If PMP entry i's A field is set to TOR, the entry matches any address y such that* **pmpaddri‑1 ≤ y < pmpaddri** *(irrespective of the value of pmpcfgi‑1)*.  
  Therefore, for entry 57, **pmpaddr57** is the upper bound and **pmpaddr56** is the lower bound of the range.

- *If pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri and pmpcfgi.A = TOR, then PMP entry i matches no addresses.*  
  Consequently, if **pmpaddr56 ≥ pmpaddr57** and **pmpcfg57.A = TOR**, entry 57 matches no addresses.

- When the **PMP granularity G ≥ 2** and **pmpcfg i .A[1] is set** (i.e., mode **NAPOT**), **bits pmpaddri[G‑2:0] read as all ones**.  
  This rule applies to **pmpaddr57** under those conditions.

- When **G ≥ 1** and **pmpcfg i .A[1] is clear** (i.e., mode **OFF** or **TOR**), **bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] read as all zeros**.  
  This rule applies to **pmpaddr57** under those conditions.

- **Bits pmpaddri[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.**  
  Hence, the low‑order **G** bits of **pmpaddr57** are ignored when **pmpcfg57.A = TOR**.

- *Although changing pmpcfgi.A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddri, it does not affect the underlying value stored in that register—in particular, **pmpaddr i [G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg i .A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT***.  
  Therefore, **pmpaddr57[G‑1]** retains its original stored bit when its configuration A field is changed between NAPOT, TOR, or OFF.

- *Software may determine the PMP granularity by writing zero to pmp0cfg, then writing all ones to pmpaddr0, then reading back pmpaddr0.*  
  This method does **not** involve **pmpaddr57**.

- **Address‑matching mode for pmpaddr61**

  *When the A field in pmpcfg61 is set to NAPOT, the low‑order bits of pmpaddr61 encode the size of the NAPOT range as shown in Table 24.*  
  *For a 4‑byte NAPOT range, pmpaddr61 = yyyy…yyyy (all low bits zero).*  
  *For an 8‑byte NAPOT range, pmpaddr61 = yyyy…yyy0 (lowest bit zero, next bit one).*  
  *For a 16‑byte NAPOT range, pmpaddr61 = yyyy…yy01, and so on, with the pattern continuing up to the maximum 2 XLEN+3‑byte range (pmpaddr61 = 1111…1111).*

- **Effect of PMP granularity G on bits of pmpaddr61**  
  *When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg61.A[1] is set (i.e., the mode is NAPOT), then bits pmpaddr61[G‑2:0] read as all ones.*  
  *When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg61.A[1] is clear (i.e., the mode is OFF or TOR), then bits pmpaddr61[G‑1:0] read as all zeros.*  
  *Bits pmpaddr61[G‑1:0] do not affect the TOR address‑matching logic.*

- **Retention of underlying value when A[1] changes**  
  *Changing pmpcfg61.A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddr61, but does not affect the underlying value stored in that register; in particular, pmpaddr61[G‑1] retains its original value when pmpcfg61.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT.*

============================================================

RULE 6: For an 8‑byte NAPOT range, the least significant bit of pmpaddr61 is zero and the next least significant bit is one.

The following description:

- **Read‑modify‑write semantics of CSRRS/CSRRC on pmpaddr63**  
  *The source states:* "Since CSRRS and CSRRC perform a read‑modify‑write operation, any bits that read as a different value to their underlying value may be modified by these instructions even if the corresponding bit is not set in rs1. Executing CSRRC or CSRRS to modify a different bit will cause 0 to be read from **pmpaddrn[G‑1]** and then written back, updating the underlying value to 0."  
  *Interpretation for pmpaddr63:* The same behavior applies to **pmpaddr63** (where n = 63). Bit G‑1 of pmpaddr63 may be stored as 1 but read as 0. If a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction changes any other bit of pmpaddr63, the read will return the mismatched value for bit G‑1 and the instruction will write that value back, thereby updating the underlying value of bit G‑1 to the read value (e.g., 0).

- **CSRRS and CSRRC always perform a read of the addressed CSR**  
  *The source states:* "Both CSRRS and CSRRC always read the addressed CSR and cause any read side effects regardless of rs1 and rd fields."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr63:* Any CSRRS or CSRRC instruction that targets pmpaddr63 will read pmpaddr63 and any read side effects associated with that CSR will occur, independent of the values in rs1 or rd.

- **Write suppression when rs1 = x0 for CSRRS/CSRRC**  
  *The source states:* "For both CSRRS and CSRRC, if rs1 = x0, then the instruction will not write to the CSR at all, and so shall not cause any of the side effects that might otherwise occur on a CSR write, nor raise illegal‑instruction exceptions on accesses to read‑only CSRs."  
  *Effect on pmpaddr63:* When a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction with rs1 = x0 targets pmpaddr63, the instruction reads pmpaddr63 but does **not** write to it, and no write‑side effects are produced.

- **Table 7 rules that directly affect pmpaddr63**  

  | Instruction | rs1 is x0? | Reads CSR? | Writes CSR? |
  |------------|------------|------------|-------------|
  | CSRRS/CSRRC| Yes        | Yes        | No          |
  | CSRRS/CSRRC| No         | Yes        | Yes         |

  *Interpretation:* For pmpaddr63, a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction with rs1 = x0 reads pmpaddr63 but does not write it; with rs1 ≠ x0 it both reads and writes pmpaddr63.
============================================================

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================

RULE 2: Bit G‑1 of pmpaddr63 may be stored as 1 but read as 0.  

RULE 3: Any CSRRS or CSRRC instruction that targets pmpaddr63 shall read pmpaddr63 and shall cause any read side effects associated with pmpaddr63 regardless of the values in rs1 or rd.  

RULE 4: When a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction with rs1 = x0 targets pmpaddr63, the instruction shall not write to pmpaddr63, shall not cause any write‑side effects on pmpaddr63, and shall not raise an illegal‑instruction exception for a read‑only access to pmpaddr63.  

RULE 5: For pmpaddr63, a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction with rs1 not equal to x0 shall both read pmpaddr63 and write pmpaddr63.  

RULE 6: For pmpaddr63, a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction with rs1 = x0 shall read pmpaddr63 and shall not write pmpaddr63.

| pmpaddr pattern | pmpcfg.A | Match type and size |
|-----------------|----------|---------------------|

| yyyy…yyy0       | NAPOT    | 8‑byte NAPOT range |
| yyyy…yy01       | NAPOT    | 16‑byte NAPOT range |
| yyyy…y011       | NAPOT    | 32‑byte NAPOT range |
| …               | …        | … |
| yy01…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN‑byte NAPOT range |
| y011…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+1‑byte NAPOT range |
| 0111…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+2‑byte NAPOT range |
| 1111…1111       | NAPOT    | 2 XLEN+3‑byte NAPOT range |

The entry matches any address *y* such that **pmpaddr62 ≤ y < pmpaddr63** (irrespective of the value of **pmpcfg62**).

- If **pmpcfg0.A = TOR**, zero is used for the lower bound, and the entry matches any address *y* < **pmpaddr0**. (This rule applies analogously to entry 63 when it is entry 0.)

- If **pmpaddri‑1 ≥ pmpaddri** and **pmpcfgi.A = TOR**, then PMP entry *i* (including entry 63) matches no addresses.

- "It is not possible to represent the address 2 XLEN+2 as the top of a range… a TOR PMP cannot be used to give less‑privileged modes access to the uppermost word of memory." (Applies to any TOR entry, including one that would use **pmpaddr63** as the top.)

- The PMP grain is **2 G+2 bytes** and must be the same across all PMP regions. When **G ≥ 1**, the **NA4** mode is not selectable. (Thus **pmpaddr63** cannot be used in NA4 mode when G ≥ 1.)

- When **G ≥ 2** and **pmpcfg63.A[1]** is set (i.e., the mode is **NAPOT**), then bits **pmpaddr63[G‑2:0]** read as all ones.

- When **G ≥ 1** and **pmpcfg63.A[1]** is clear (i.e., the mode is **OFF** or **TOR**), then bits **pmpaddr63[G‑1:0]** read as all zeros.

The following description:

- **Effect of `mseccfg.RLB` on `pmpcfg.L`**  
  *When `mseccfg.RLB` is 0 and `pmpcfg.L` is 1 in any rule or entry (including disabled entries), then `mseccfg.RLB` remains 0 and any further modifications to `mseccfg.RLB` are ignored until a PMP reset.*  

- **Effect of `mseccfg.MML` on the meaning of `pmpcfg.L`**  
  *When `mseccfg.MML` is set, the meaning of `pmpcfg.L` changes: instead of marking a rule as locked and enforced in all modes, it now marks a rule as M‑mode‑only when set and S/U‑mode‑only when unset.*  

- **Effect of `mseccfg.MML` on previously reserved encodings**  
  *When `mseccfg.MML` is set, the formerly reserved encoding of `pmpcfg.RW=01`, and the encoding `pmpcfg.LRWX=1111`, now encode a Shared‑Region.*  

- **Shared‑Region rules (enabled by `mseccfg.MML`)**  
  *A Shared‑Region rule is enforced on all modes, with restrictions depending on the `pmpcfg.L` and `pmpcfg.X` bits:*  
  • *If `pmpcfg.L` is not set, the rule can be used for sharing data between M‑mode and S/U‑mode; it is not executable. M‑mode has read/write access; S/U‑mode has read access if `pmpcfg.X` is not set, or read/write access if `pmpcfg.X` is set.*  
  • *If `pmpcfg.L` is set, the rule can be used for sharing code between M‑mode and S/U‑mode; it is not writable. Both M‑mode and S/U‑mode have execute access, and M‑mode also has read access if `pmpcfg.X` is set.*  
  • *If `pmpcfg.LRWX=1111`, the rule can be used for sharing data between M‑mode and S/U‑mode, where both modes have only read‑only access.*  

- **Lock behavior of M‑mode‑only and Shared‑Region rules**  
  *An M‑mode‑only rule is enforced on Machine mode and denied in Supervisor or User mode. It also remains locked so that any further modifications to its associated configuration or address registers are ignored until a PMP reset, unless `mseccfg.RLB` is set.*  
  *A locked Shared‑Region rule (i.e., a Shared‑Region rule with `pmpcfg.L` set) also remains locked under the same condition.*  

- **Effect of `mseccfg.MML` on writeability of `pmpcfg`**  
  *Adding a rule with executable privileges that either is M‑mode‑only or a locked Shared‑Region is not possible and such `pmpcfg` writes are ignored, leaving `pmpcfg` unchanged. This restriction can be temporarily lifted by setting `mseccfg.RLB`.*  

- **Effect of `mseccfg.MML` on execution permission checks**

The following description:

- **CSR name and existence**  
  - The CSR **pmpcfg0** is one of the PMP configuration registers.  
  - For RV32 implementations there are sixteen CSRs, **pmpcfg0‑pmpcfg15**, that "hold the configurations pmp0cfg‑pmp63cfg for the 64 PMP entries" (Figure 30).  
  - For RV64 implementations there are eight even‑numbered CSRs, **pmpcfg0, pmpcfg2, …, pmpcfg14**, that "hold the configurations for the 64 PMP entries" (Figure 31).

- **Access permissions for the CSR**  
  - "PMP CSRs are only accessible to M‑mode."  
  - Therefore any read or write of **pmpcfg0** must be performed in M‑mode; accesses from lower privilege modes are not permitted.

- **Field characteristics**  
  - "All PMP CSR fields are **WARL** and may be read‑only zero."  
  - Consequently each field within **pmpcfg0** (R, W, X, A, L) is a WARL field and can read back as zero even if written with a different value.

  - The **R**, **W**, **X** fields form a collective WARL field "for which the combinations with R = 0 and W = 1 are reserved."  
  - The remaining two fields, **A** and **L**, are described elsewhere but are part of the same register.

- **Effect of the permission bits configured in pmpcfg0**  
  - **Execute permission (X bit)**: "Attempting to fetch an instruction from a PMP region that does not have execute permissions raises an **instruction access‑fault exception**."  
  - **Read permission (R bit)**: "Attempting to execute a load, load‑reserved, or cache‑block management instruction which accesses a physical address within a PMP region without read permissions raises a **load access‑fault exception**."  
  - **Write permission (W bit)**: "Attempting to execute a store, store‑conditional, AMO, or cache‑block zero instruction which accesses a physical address within a PMP region without write permissions raises a **store access‑fault exception**."
